November 9, 2026




 Page strikes gold! 

Jamaican smashes Youth Olympic record in 110m hurdles 






KINGSTON, Jamaica— Marquies Page won Jamaica’s first gold medal at the Youth Olympic Games that are being held at Stade Iba Mar Diop in Dakar, Senegal on Monday, running a personal best and Youth Olympic record 12.95 seconds (-0.4m/s) to win the 110m hurdles final.

Page was the second Jamaican to win the event and broke the previous record 12.96 seconds that was set by compatriot Jaheel Hyde in Nanjing, China in 2014.

Page’s previous best in the event was 13.06 seconds which he ran while winning the Class 2 boys’ 110m hurdles at the ISSA Boys’ and Girls’ Champs in March.

The 16- year-old page who was a semi-finalist at the World Under- 20 Championships at Hayward Field in Eugene, Oregon in August, beat China’s Shijie Chen who took the silver medal in a personal best 13.40 seconds, while Enrique Bosch of South Africa won the bronze medal with 13.45 seconds.

In the preliminaries, Page had won his heat in 13.20 seconds (-0.1m/s), again ahead of China’s Chen.

— Paul A Reid

 Estrada, Hastings set up thrilling final round of Jamaica Golf Open 







TRYALL, Hanover— The stage has been set for an exciting final day of the 58th Vybwear Jamaica Golf Open at Tryall Club on Tuesday after Nicholas Estrada of the USA and Justin Hastings of the Cayman Islands finished Monday’s second round tied on nine under par 135.

Both men who teed off in the final group, shot three under for the day, the same score carded by Canadian Ty Celone who is in third place on a two round score of three under 141, tied with first day leader Tyler Stachkunas who shot a four over 76.

There is a bottle neck behind the joint leaders with six players, separated by two shots including Mac McClair who had the highest of highs with back-to-back eagles on the front nine which he played in five under and the lowest of lows with a bogie and double bogie on back-to-back holes on the back nine.

Jamaica’s Justin Burrowes was one under par 143 and was in eighth place going into the final round while Wesley Brown shot a two under 70 after carding a seven over 79 on the first day.

Hastings who had shot a 66 on the first day was not happy with his execution on Monday but was able to save himself with his putter on more than one occasion.

Justin Hastings

“It was a little bit sloppier than yesterday. I putted really poorly on the front nine and was able to hit some good shots and turn at a decent score,” he said. “And then, you know the back nine it kind of flipped. I started hitting some weird shots and and saving myself with the putter. So a little bit sloppier but I hope to execute a little bit better tomorrow. And yeah, we’ll see where it gets us.”

Monday, he said, had different conditions than Sunday.

“We got a little bit more wind today. Some different pin locations. So you know seeing it for the first time this week, I’m seeing different sides of the golf course, but yeah, it’s like I said yesterday its a great test, and you know it’s gonna reward you for hitting good shots, but it’s really gonna punish you for hitting bad shots. So I think it’s just about going out there and executing, you know, the best you can, and adding it up at the end,” he argued.

Estrada described the conditions as a struggle.

“I want to thank God because it is a fight out there, my game feels a little bit off, especially those last six holes. I mean, the wind starts picking up, the course is really tight, and my swing didn’t feel all there, but we were able to put it together, and I’m very happy with where I’m at, and gives me a good position to go get at them tomorrow,” he said.

Estrada who says he is mentored by the 1958 winner, American Bob Toski who turned 100 recently, said he had the title on his mind.

“I’m going out there to win. I’m going to leave it all out on the table and hopefully walk away with the trophy,” he said.

Hastings got into trouble early when he shot a double bogie on the par three second hole but rallied to birdie four of the next five holes to play the first nine holes in two under par.

He then bogied the 10th home followed by an eagle on the 11th hole to finish at three under for the day.

Estrada had two birdies and a bogie on the front nine but stepped it up on the back nine with four birdies and two bogies.

Celone who was even on the first day, put himself in contention with a steady round to be tied with Stachkunas who followed up a seven under on Sunday with a nightmare back nine on Monday where he had four bogies and a triple bogie, carding seven on the par four 18th hole.

 Teen dies in suspected drowning during early morning swim in St Toolies River 







MANCHESTER, Jamaica — A 17-year-old is suspected to have drowned during an early morning swim with his friends in the St Toolies River.

Police named him as Tyrone Williams, a resident of Grove Town district in Manchester.

A police report said about 6:15 am Williams and a group of friends went swimming at St Toolies River on the Manchester/ Clarendon border when he got into difficulty and attempts to save him were unsuccessful.

Police were called in, and the body was retrieved from the river. He was pronounced dead at hospital.

This latest incident follows a suspected case of drowning involving another man in Alligator Pond, Manchester on Saturday.

The vehicle reportedly went to pick up money from a popular fast food establishment when the heist occurred. 

It is still to be officially confirmed, but it is alleged that armed guards exited the vehicle when it arrived at the popular fast food establishment on Hope Road to pick up the yield for the day. 

While that was happening, the thieves hijacked the vehicle and made off with money that the couriers had previously picked up for the day from other establishments.

 WATCH: KSAMC rolls out new parking arrangements for taxi operators 







KINGSTON, Jamaica—The Kingston and St Andrew Municipal Corporation is rolling out new parking arrangements for taxi operators in Downtown Kingston, in a move to ease traffic congestion and improve road safety.

The new parking arrangements are expected to begin as a pilot project, with over 2,500 taxi operators expected to benefit from the rollout.

“Myself and my team have been lobbying for parking downtown for well over seven years. But over the past two years and some months, we have been, with this new mayor, we have been going at pace, actually on a monthly basis and therefore, the hard work he has put in with the KSAC team has paid off today and I think we have more to do. We’re coming to Half-Way -Tree and Papine shortly, but right now we’re going to focus on downtown to see what can be done in terms of discipline, and then we’ll move to other areas,” said Edgerton Newman, president of TODSS, Transport Operators Development Sustainable Services.

He described the pilot project as an historic moment for transport operators in the Kingston Metropolitan Transport Region (KMTR) and in downtown Kingston, particularly.

“What was said by the mayor [Andrew Swaby] today is, one that gives us hope that a change is coming for the transport sector and if we continue on this trend, of course, the 2030 vision will be upheld by the public transport sector. So we want to thank the mayor and his team for sticking with us, sticking to the task ahead. And today we can say to our operators, come tomorrow morning, zero tolerance. We have to do our part,” he added.

Meanwhile, Mayor of Kingston Andrew Swaby said the initiative is particularly important in bringing law and order to the shopping district.

“We have to have some law and order in the city. I’m starting right there. I’m tired of driving down Upper King Street and taxi man them block up the road, two side of the road,” he noted.

He noted that this is particularly important as it gets closer to the festive season.

“We want to make sure that we go into the Christmas season in a little bit more order downtown because the normal person they’re not coming to shop in a chaos. So what we are trying to do is organise the place in a way where more patrons will come downtown and will utilise your service because you know that there’s chaos also, pickpocketing, extortion, and all of those things take place,” he said.

news.title: PSX: stocks surge, KSE-100 gains over 2%
news.text:
Buying returned at the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) after US President Donald Trump said US military action against Iran ​is not necessary “at this point”, with the benchmark KSE-100 gaining over 2% points during the opening hours of trading on Tuesday.

At 10:50am, the benchmark index was hovering at 177,374.56, up 3,487.88 points or 2.01%.

Buying was observed in key sectors, including automobile assemblers, cement, commercial banks, oil and gas exploration companies, OMCs and power generation. Index-heavy stocks, including MARI, OGDC, PPL, PSO, HUBCO, HBL, MCB, MEBL and UBL, traded in the green.

The PSX recorded its strongest weekly rally in nearly six months, with the benchmark KSE-100 Index surging 7,477.44 points, or 4.5% week-on-week, to close at 173,886.69 points.

Globally, Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he plans to hold off on new military strikes ​against Iran lifted sentiment ahead of US inflation data that could sway the near-term interest rate outlook.

Brent crude futures were hovering at their lowest ‌levels since early September, well below $100 per barrel, as investors pinned their hopes on possible talks between US and Iran.

They were last down 1% at $91.56 a barrel.

The US-Israeli war with Iran, which erupted at the end of February, has stoked inflationary concerns across the globe, spurring major central banks to raise rates in recent months.

Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global, said the latest ​developments offered hope that an end to the conflict could be approaching, but there was still a considerable gap between diplomacy and a lasting ​peace agreement.

The slump in oil prices eased inflation worries and helped lift stocks after last ​week’s rout as a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

South Korea’s ​KOSPI rose over 5%, while Japan’s Nikkei gained about 3% in early trading. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares pushed 1.5% higher, moving away from the seven-month low it hit last week.

On Monday, the S&P 500 clocked its biggest one-day jump since April, closing up 2.35% while the Nasdaq closed 2.7% higher, its best day in over four months.

Earnings ​reports due this week from tech companies including CoreWeave, a barometer of investor anxiety over AI, will be another test for markets as investors fret about the cost of the ‌AI buildout.

This is an intraday update

news.title: Pentagon chief Hegseth expected to face House impeachment vote this week
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Pete Hegseth, the US defense secretary, calls himself the secretary of war, part of his effort to rebrand a military he said was too weak and “woke” when ​he took office last year. Now, with an expected House impeachment vote this week, he could soon share something in common with an actual secretary of war.

William Belknap, who held that title in 1876, became the first, and to date only, civilian leader of the US military to be impeached by Congress.

US Representative Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican, introduced eight articles of impeachment on Monday, setting off a two-day clock for a potential House vote on charges including waging war against Iran without congressional approval and other abuses of power.

Massie, addressing reporters, cautioned that Republican leadership could try to avoid a straight vote on impeachment by trying to dismiss it with a procedural motion.

“They may try to get out of an actual vote on the substance of this. We should have a vote and a rigorous debate on these eight articles of impeachment,” he told a press conference.

Congressional sources say the resolution may have ‌the votes to pass ‌even with President Donald Trump’s Republicans still controlling the House until Democrats take over on January ​3. Conviction ‌appears ⁠unlikely in ​the ⁠Senate, however, where a two-thirds majority is required and Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats.

President Donald Trump, in an interview with Reuters on Monday, strongly defended Hegseth, pointing to the US military’s performance in Iran and Venezuela: “Well, he won two wars. I don’t know how you can impeach him.” He later told a White House press conference he would stand by Hegseth even if he is impeached, and called Massie a “stone-cold loser.”

House Speaker Mike Johnson opposed the effort, saying impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad” would be “a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see.”

Voter anger over the war helped Democrats win control of Congress in last week’s midterm elections, intensifying Republican divisions over a conflict that Vice President JD Vance has publicly questioned and Hegseth has defended as “courageous and historic.”

Accused of taking huge kickbacks, ⁠Belknap handed President Ulysses Grant his resignation ahead of his scheduled impeachment vote and, according to a Senate history, “burst ‌into tears.” The House impeached him anyway, but the Senate later acquitted him after falling short of ‌the required two-thirds majority.

By contrast, Hegseth is promising to stay and fight.

Hegseth says he ​is not worried

Hegseth has mounted a social media campaign, saying in ‌a defiant video message last week that he would not back down. He also drew a comparison to Trump, who was impeached twice, saying: “It didn’t ‌work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me.”

Asked if he had enough Republican support to defeat the impeachment push, Hegseth said on Monday: “We’re not worried about that.” He announced a Tuesday press conference, his first at the Pentagon since May.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also White House national security adviser, called the impeachment push “unfair,” telling reporters: “I think Pete’s done a good job. I really do.”

Trump, speaking with Reuters, extolled Hegseth’s performance in the Iran war, which is at an impasse, and with Venezuela, where ‌the US military deposed that country’s president, Nicolás Maduro, in a surprise January commando raid on his compound in the Venezuelan capital.

“Well, what about impeaching the people from Vietnam, Afghanistan, Iraq and all of that, ⁠where we fought forever and nothing happened?” ⁠Trump asked.

Defense spending at risk?

Some Republican lawmakers have expressed concern that if Hegseth stays, his strained relationship with Congress will undermine the Trump administration’s push for a $1.5 trillion defense spending package.

Massie, a Trump critic who is leaving office in January, warned in a statement on Monday that impeachment would be “much gentler” than what’s in store for Hegseth once Democrats take control in January.

“They will hold hearings and trials. President Trump should replace Secretary Hegseth now while he can still get a replacement confirmed in the Senate,” Massie said.

Democrats have promised to investigate Hegseth over issues including the firing of the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff and other senior leaders.

House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries said on Sunday he was a “hard yes” on a measure to impeach Hegseth.

US Senator Chuck Schumer, a New York Democrat who is expected to become majority leader, said on Monday the Senate needs to put Hegseth on trial.

“Hegseth waged this war illegally, in open defiance of the Constitution and multiple War Powers Resolutions this Congress passed to end the fighting,” he said.

Massie’s articles of impeachment accuse Hegseth of “high crimes and misdemeanors” ranging from waging the Iran war to various alleged abuses of power, including violating the free speech rights of US Senator ​Mark Kelly, an Arizona Democrat.

Last year, Hegseth sought to prosecute Kelly ​after he and five other Democrats in Congress with backgrounds in the military and intelligence urged US troops to refuse illegal orders. Hegseth accused them of sedition, something Trump at the time said in a social media post was “punishable by DEATH!”

 November 9, 2026




 NEPA to release 1,000th Jamaican iguana into the wild 







The thousandth Jamaican rock iguana is set to be released into the wild on Saturday, marking a major milestone in the island’s decades-long conservation programme for the critically endangered reptile.

Environmental enthusiasts gathered at Jamaica Pegasus on Monday for the annual meeting of the conservation community ahead of the historic release, which Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda described as a significant achievement in Jamaica’s efforts to protect the species.

“This historic milestone is not to be taken lightly. The thousandth head-started Jamaican iguana into the wild … is a big deal,” Samuda said.

The Jamaican rock iguana was declared extinct in 1948 before being rediscovered in 1990. Since then, more than 30 years of scientific research, habitat management, captive rearing, predator control and reintroduction efforts have helped restore the population.

Samuda said the Jamaican Iguana Recovery Programme was now internationally recognised as a conservation success story, with each lizard returned to its natural habitat representing years of scientific work and the commitment of individuals and institutions.

He highlighted the work being done in the Hellshire Hills to protect the remaining wild population, including monitoring nesting sites and controlling invasive predators such as Indian mongooses and feral cats. More than 280 live predator traps are currently monitored, with more than 1,500 predators removed from the iguana’s core habitat over time.

Minister of Water, Environment and Climate Change Matthew Samuda (second left) makes a point in discussion with (from left) National Environment and Planning Agency CEO Leonard Francis; Senior Researcher at the University of the Valley of Guatemala, Daniel Ariano; and Conservation Biologist at Fort Worth Zoo, Stesha Pasachnik at the Iguana Specialist Group Meeting at the Jamaica Pegasus on Monday, November 9, 2026. (Photo: Karl McLarty)

At Hope Zoo, the head-start programme cares for approximately 250 to 300 juvenile iguanas, raising them in a protected environment until they are large enough to have a better chance of surviving in the wild.

The minister also outlined the Government’s plans to increase protected areas as part of Jamaica’s environmental management strategy. He said the country had already protected slightly more than 25 per cent of its landmass and was aiming to surpass the 30 per cent target within the next fiscal year and a half, ahead of the 2030 international deadline.

Jamaica’s protected marine areas currently account for approximately 13.5 per cent of its Exclusive Economic Zone, but Samuda said further increases were planned.

He also acknowledged the fiscal challenges following Hurricane Melissa but assured conservationists and environmental agencies, including the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), that there would be significant increases in provisions for conservation and restoration work in the coming fiscal year.

Speaking with Observer Online, Iguana Conservation Specialist Tandora Del Grant, who has been involved in the project since 1995, described the upcoming release as an encouraging milestone.

“It’s a nice milestone. It gives us a good feeling that we are being successful and the animals in the wild are surviving and reproducing on their own,” she said.

However, Del Grant cautioned that the work was far from over, noting that conservation efforts would need to continue to prevent the population from declining again.

She identified the eventual reintroduction of the iguanas to Goat Island as the next major milestone, explaining that the island could serve as another sanctuary and head-start facility for the Hellshire Hills population.

She also expressed hope that Jamaicans would embrace the iguana as a flagship for the country’s conservation efforts, describing it as an international success story.

NEPA ranger and member of the Iguana Recovery Team Oneil Wilson said the programme’s progress was particularly rewarding, having been involved for more than seven years.

“The process is very rigorous in terms of the repopulation of Jamaican rock iguana. It’s a very daunting task, but it’s rewarding,” he said.

Another member of the team, NEPA ranger Jomo Pinkney, highlighted the species’ importance to the environment, explaining that iguanas help with the regeneration of trees by dispersing seeds after eating fruit.

The Hellshire Hills is home to the Caribbean’s largest dry forest, making the iguanas’ role in seed dispersal particularly important to the area’s regeneration.

A total of 114 additional iguanas are scheduled to be released into the wild on Saturday, taking the programme beyond the 1,000-animal milestone, with 973 already released.

news.title: Russia, Ukraine, and the US Resume Talks After a Long Pause. What to Expect from the Meeting in Abu Dhabi?
news.text:
What is planned for discussion at the talks

Before the start of the talks, the authorities of Russia, Ukraine, and the USA made it clear that they would primarily discuss security issues — affecting not only Moscow and Kyiv but also all of Europe.

A few days before the talks, Donald Trump met with Russia's President's special representative Kirill Dmitriev in Washington. After the conversation, Trump expressed confidence that a "great excellent agreement" would soon be concluded. His son-in-law Jared Kushner clarified: it's about a new architecture of European security and security guarantees for Ukraine and Russia. Washington intends to discuss these proposals, including in Abu Dhabi.

Russian authorities confirmed that they plan to discuss security guarantees in the UAE.

"The agenda of the Abu Dhabi talks itself provides as the first point issues of security for Russia, Ukraine, and security in this region in general," said Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov. "We only welcome such an approach."

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had named other topics as Kyiv's main priorities at the beginning of November: a possible freezing of hostilities and an energy truce, de-escalation in the Black Sea, humanitarian exchanges, and organizing a meeting at the leaders' level. He later clarified that Kyiv is ready to talk about security guarantees, but primarily those concerning Ukraine itself, not all of Europe.

Who is going to Abu Dhabi

There will be no radical changes in the composition of the participants in the trilateral talks. The talks on behalf of the USA will be conducted by Donald Trump's special representative Steve Witkoff and US President's son-in-law Jared Kushner. In the weeks leading up to the meeting, they managed to visit Russia and Ukraine and hold talks with European allies.

The Ukrainian team at the talks will be headed by Rustem Umerov, head of the Foreign Intelligence Service. It will also include David Arakhamia, head of the "Servant of the People" party faction, Kyrylo Budanov, head of the President's Office, his deputy Serhiy Kyslytsia, and Vadym Skibitsky, deputy head of military intelligence.

The Russian delegation will again be led by Russian President's aide Vladimir Medinsky. He will travel to Abu Dhabi with a large team, which will include two deputy heads of the Foreign Ministry — Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, as well as representatives of two departments of the General Staff of the Russian Armed Forces — Igor Kostyukov and Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Among these negotiators, only Ryabkov has not previously participated in contacts in the trilateral format. His appearance in the delegation can be explained by the agenda of the Abu Dhabi meeting. In 2021, it was Ryabkov who coordinated the negotiations on security demands that Russia presented to the West shortly before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

At that time, Moscow ultimatum-style demanded from Washington a refusal to expand NATO eastward and the withdrawal of all armed forces and infrastructure from the territories of countries that joined the alliance after 1997. Ryabkov, as a participant in these negotiations, stated in an interview that NATO should "pack its bags."

The White House then agreed to discuss some issues — for example, arms control, but rejected the Kremlin's toughest demands.

Why Europeans are going to Abu Dhabi

According to the Financial Times, the new US proposals caught the Europeans by surprise. They are sending their representatives to Abu Dhabi so that discussions about the continent's security do not take place without their participation.

"In recent weeks, Europeans have made themselves heard; they have made it clear to the American mediator that no discussion concerning the future of the continent can ignore our expectations and demands," French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on the eve of the meeting. "France will defend Europe's position, as this issue affects it first and foremost."

According to Euronews and Le Monde, national security advisors from the UK, Germany, and France will arrive in Abu Dhabi. Representatives from Italy are also expected. NATO will be represented by the Chief of Staff of the Alliance's Secretary General, Geoffrey van Leeuwen; the European Commission by the Chief of Staff of its President, Björn Seibert; and the European Council by the advisor to its President, Ana-Maria Burra.

This is the first time talks have taken place with such broad European participation. However, they will not be directly at the meeting, Russian and Ukrainian authorities stated.

"We will hold separate coordination meetings with European partners," explained the head of the Ukrainian delegation, Umerov. "As determined by President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, we are doing everything to ensure Europe is a participant in the diplomatic process."

Dmitry Peskov, the press secretary of the Russian president, emphasized that the negotiations would be precisely "trilateral."

"As for the presence of Europeans, you know that Americans have their own communication channels with Europeans, and Ukrainians have theirs with Europeans, and they, apparently, are building their own coordination mechanism," he explained.

Russian authorities have consistently opposed Europe's participation in peace talks to end the war, explaining this by the fact that Brussels provides financial and military assistance to the Ukrainian authorities. Starting from 2026, the topic of possible negotiations with Russia has been discussed in Europe several times, with European leaders still not agreeing on who could represent them in a direct dialogue with Russia.

At the end of October, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre spoke with Vladimir Putin by phone. Not everyone liked this: Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticized her colleagues for this step. Politico wrote that the call led to the "most serious rift" between Nordic countries since Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Before the start of the talks in Abu Dhabi, the Kremlin stated that Europe's participation in the peace process would be necessary sooner or later. "If there are discussions about mutual security for Russia and Ukraine, then, of course, it will be impossible to do this at some stage without Europeans," Dmitry Peskov admitted.

According to the New York Times, Russia, Ukraine, and the USA will not discuss a ceasefire at the talks. The Kremlin has repeatedly said that Moscow is not interested in pauses in hostilities before signing a full-fledged agreement on ending the war. Since early autumn, Trump has twice claimed that, through his mediation, Moscow and Kyiv allegedly agreed on an "energy truce" — that is, a refusal of mutual strikes on energy infrastructure. It never materialized.

Kushner announced before the meeting that, in addition to the plan to end the war and security issues, the parties intend to discuss Ukraine's future economic development and humanitarian measures "aimed at alleviating suffering and overcoming the severe consequences of the war for people."

news.title: ‘Chinese spy’ affair wipes $395bn off Nvidia share price
news.text:
Nvidia has lost almost $400bn (€357bn) in value after its boss admitted an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

Shares in Nvidia sank more than 8pc as trading got under way in New York on Monday, wiping more than $395bn off the value of the chip-making giant. 

The blow comes after AI fears knocked $433.8bn off the stock last week.

Investors have questioned whether Jensen Huang should continue to lead the $4.5tn semiconductor company after admitting to the affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who allegedly passed information to Beijing.

Nvidia’s board has launched an independent investigation into potential national security concerns raised by the tryst.

Dan Ives, an analyst and partner at Yorkville Ives, said: “The big question every Nvidia and tech investor is asking this morning: Will Jensen stay on as CEO of Nvidia?”

He said Nvidia’s shares sank on Monday because Mr Huang was “not replaceable” as the company’s boss.

“There is no other person on the management team bench that can step in seamlessly... Jensen has become the global face of the AI revolution for Nvidia,” he wrote in a note to clients.

Gary Black, a managing partner at The Future Fund, an Nvidia shareholder, said he expected Mr Huang to face pressure to resign.

Mr Black said Mr Huang’s “code of conduct and judgment will be called into question”, probably resulting in the board removing him from his post.

He added: “I doubt Jensen Huang will be able to remain as Nvidia chief executive.”

In a sign of the pressure on the Nvidia boss, other tech executives rallied to publicly defend him.

Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, a prominent Silicon Valley investment firm, said Mr Huang’s affair was “bad for America” but argued against replacing him.

Mr Maguire wrote on X that Mr Huang was “irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership” and added: “My guess is there was no bad intention.”

Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief executive, shared Mr Maguire’s message, adding only: “I agree.”

Bill Ackman, the Wall Street hedge fund manager, said: “Jensen Huang is human. And he is an incredible human. Even incredible humans make mistakes.

“He takes full responsibility as he should. We should all support him and his family.”

He added: “I am not suggesting he gets a free pass. If indeed this is more than an affair, then it is obviously a real problem.”

Mr Huang has in the past called for trade restrictions between China and the West to be eased. 

Luke de Pulford, head of the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China, said the revelations of his affair raised questions about this lobbying.

Mr De Pulford said: “He used his influence to oppose a tougher line on Beijing, for example, by harshly denouncing the ‘China hawk’ label as a ‘badge of shame’.

“The fact he was doing so while having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy raises the prospect of elite capture, and must be investigated.

“Nvidia’s advocacy must be treated as compromised pending investigation, and decisions taken to accommodate the company reviewed urgently.”

Beyond the questions over Mr Huang’s position at Nvidia, the company is also likely to face shareholder lawsuits.

Lorraine Lanceley, a partner at Stewarts, a leading UK law firm for shareholder litigation, said: “The affair itself is unlikely to be the central issue for shareholders. What matters is whether shareholders have suffered loss due to Nvidia failing to disclose material information, particularly given the sensitivities surrounding China, AI chips and US export controls.

“US plaintiff lawyers will be looking closely at matters such as what Nvidia and its board knew and when, what was said publicly and whether any material information was withheld from the market.”

In a message to staff on Sunday, Mr Huang said he was “deeply sorry”, after confirming that he had been in a romantic relationship with Ms Huang.

Mr Huang said: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Nvidia previously denied claims of an inappropriate relationship between Mr Huang and the suspected Chinese spy.

US authorities have reportedly been investigating Ms Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based company Megaspeed, which buys AI semiconductor chips from Nvidia.

Megaspeed has been suspected of helping Beijing to gain access to advanced AI chips that are banned from being exported to China.

In a statement late last year, a Megaspeed spokesman denied wrongdoing.

He said: “We operate fully within the bounds of all applicable export control regulations and maintain the highest standards of legal and ethical conduct.”

China has also denied that Ms Huang is a spy for Beijing, calling it “nothing but smears against China”.

Mr Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 as a company designing and manufacturing specialist graphics-processing units, known as GPUs, for the gaming industry.

However, he made the decision to refocus the company on making AI chips in the early 2010s. The early bet helped Nvidia become a world leader in manufacturing the high-powered chips needed to power products such as OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude.

US president Donald Trump imposed a ban on Nvidia selling its most advanced H200 chips to China last year.

news.title: Oil prices fall to two-month low as Donald Trump says new Iran strikes ‘unlikely’
news.text:
Oil prices have fallen to a fresh two-month low as optimism among investors over signs of diplomacy between the US and Iran helped the sell-off gain steam.

The price of Brent crude oil fell by more than 4pc to below $93 a barrel on Monday afternoon.

This took the commodity to its lowest price since early September. 

It had edged back up to around $94 a barrel shortly after.

The price of Brent crude has tumbled from highs of more than $115 a barrel late last month, as investors welcomed signs of diplomatic efforts between the US and Iran.

US president Donald Trump recognised last week that the Iran war played a part in his Republican Party’s defeat in the mid-term elections but said it was something he had to do.

Over the weekend, the president dialled down his previous tone towards the conflict and said he was “highly unlikely” to order new strikes in Iran should talks progress, including around the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

Oil prices have spiked since the start of the war in late February because of concerns about supply constraints in the Middle East, and have remained significantly above their pre-conflict levels.

Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist for Wealth Club, said: “Investors are assessing signs of progress in Middle East peace negotiations after Trump’s latest comments suggesting fresh attacks on Iran are highly unlikely, while talks continue.”

She said “hopes of a more conciliatory approach help take some of the heat out of oil markets”.

Chris Beauchamp, chief market analyst for IG, said: “Two-month lows in oil have done much to bolster bruised sentiment in global markets, and the admittedly small signs of progress in peace talks adds to downward move.

“Each passing day adds to the view that no resumption of the war is likely, but one more US carrier is yet to arrive in-region, adding a hefty dose of uncertainty.”

news.title: Ukraine will have a different shape after war, says Trump ahead of peace talks
news.text:
Ukraine will have a “different shape” after the war, Donald Trump has said before peace talks this week.

In an ominous sign for Kyiv, the US president refused to spell out whether Ukraine would emerge free and independent from the long-running conflict.

His comments began what was expected to be a frantic two weeks of US-led diplomacy to end the Russia-Ukraine and Iran wars.

As well as talks between officials from Kyiv, Moscow and Washington in Abu Dhabi, Mr Trump said he would address both conflicts with Russia’s Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping on the fringes of a summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Diplomats and officials in European capitals have quietly raised concerns about the prospect that the US president, bruised by his Republican Party’s thrashing in the mid-term elections, could seek uncomfortable deals with Moscow and Beijing to end the wars.

“I think we’re going to have it done, and I think it’s going to happen, and they’re going to end up with a little bit different shape [for] Ukraine,” Mr Trump told CBS News’s 60 Minutes, speaking about his expectations for the trilateral talks in the United Arab Emirates.

Officials involved in the talks have often described the future of Russian-occupied territory in Ukraine as the hardest issue to overcome in the US-mediated peace negotiations.

Moscow controls about 20pc of Ukraine, mostly in its eastern Donbas regions of Donetsk and Luhansk.

Putin has so far refused any suggestion of a ceasefire unless Kyiv withdraws its forces from the two oblasts, while Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine’s president, argues he cannot cede the territories under his country’s laws.

“There’s a very important meeting taking place,” Mr Trump said. “I believe that that war is going to end and it’s going to end soon. And the only reason it’s going to end is because of me.”

Asked what he believed was the main obstacle to a peace agreement, the US president blamed the relationship between the warring leaders.

“It was the hatred between Zelensky and Putin,” Mr Trump said. He added: “When [they] had their first meeting, there was great disrespect shown to Russia... So I’m not going to say anything.”

Rather than tackling territorial issues, the talks in Abu Dhabi are expected to focus on security architecture with Europe. Jared Kushner, Mr Trump’s son-in-law and peace envoy, is expected to push for the resumption of the Nato-Russia Council, a joint body used for escalation management.

It has seldom met since 2014, when Russia illegally annexed the Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea, but was once used to detail planned military exercises and conversations over non-proliferation strategies.

European officials have signalled a willingness to discuss the resumption of communication channels with Moscow after a ceasefire is brokered.

But it is expected that Putin will use the talks as an attempt to renew his push for Nato to withdraw troops and weapons from Eastern Europe.

The Kremlin said on Monday that European officials would not be involved in the talks. Instead, it is expected that British, French, German, EU and Nato officials will be briefed by the Americans on any progress.

On the conflict with Iran, Mr Trump told CBS News that there was “no reason” to escalate the war with renewed strikes against the Islamic Republic.

Further military action could lead to an all-out war, driving up fuel prices further, which was one of the key reasons for his mid-term defeat.

The US president was due to meet Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani, the Qatari prime minister, who has been mediating talks between Washington and Tehran, in the Oval Office on Monday.

It is understood the Qataris are confident that a deal to end the fighting is drawing closer because of Iran’s perceived willingness to shut down a number of its nuclear production facilities.

But Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, warned the talks were not “at the verge of a breakthrough” because Tehran’s demands were unacceptable.

“Right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic,” Mr Rubio told reporters before flying to Paris for a meeting of G7 ministers.

Masoud Pezeshkian, the Iranian president, said the supreme leader had ordered an end to the current limbo, signalling that Tehran was prepared to negotiate its way out of the conflict with the US and Israel.

“The supreme leader has ordered us to end the no war, no peace situation,” Mr Pezeshkian said on Monday.

He added: “We can hold talks with dignity and end the matter with dignity. We are people of dialogue and negotiation, and logic dictates that if we can secure our rights through talks, we should not drag ourselves into war — but we will not surrender to force and bullying either.” (© Telegraph Media Group Holdings Ltd)

news.title: ‘Urgency of the moment must drive us forward,’ say leaders as COP31 climate summit begins
news.text:
Leaders of COP31 urged the world to accelerate the fight against global warming as they began their annual UN climate conference in Turkey on Monday against a backdrop of rising temperatures and worsening climate-driven disasters.

Kicking off two weeks of debate at Antalya on Turkey’s Mediterranean coast, UN and government leaders emphasised the need to focus on climate as it competes for attention with other international crises, including war, soaring inflation and the uncertainties caused by artificial intelligence (AI).

“The urgency of this moment must drive us forward,” UN Climate Change executive secretary Simon Stiell said, adding progress so far was “nowhere near fast enough”.

A report by the United Nations Environment Programme published last month said the world was already poised to overshoot 1.5C of warming, a threshold set at the 2015 Paris climate summit, and called for steep emissions cuts.

Tina Stege, COP31 climate envoy for the Marshall Islands and regional envoy for Oceania, said acting now was essential. 

“For Pacific Island countries, this is not an abstract discussion about temperature targets. It’s about people, it’s about communities, it is about the places we call home,” she told reporters.

This year is on track to be one of the four hottest on record, as a powerful El Nino has compounded the impact of global warming, a UN report showed on Monday. 

The year has been marked by a series of extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal, where resulting flood killed more than 1,450 people and left thousands more still missing.

The COP31 presidency has focused this year’s climate talks on a goal to electrify more than a third of the global economy by 2035, up from around a fifth today. 

It is asking nations to sign a pledge supporting that target.

Theoretically, it could reduce planet-warming emissions by speeding the global shift away from fossil fuel-powered vehicles, furnaces, boilers, cooking stoves, and other greenhouse gas-emitting equipment. 

“We want people to feel the results of climate talks in daily life: in buildings that use less energy, in clean public transport, in energy they can afford and in new jobs,” Turkey’s COP31 president Murat Kurum said.

But climate advocates have criticised the electrification pledge because it does not require the additional electricity to come from low-carbon sources, setting up an early fight over whether electrification alone should count as climate progress.

The US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine have highlighted the economic consequences of continued dependency on fossil fuels as high prices linked to disruption have driven inflation higher.

While climate campaigners say the obvious solution is to increase use of renewable power, the oil and gas industry has made big profits and some countries that have domestic reserves of fossil fuel have sought to increase output.

US president Donald Trump’s administration – which is staying away from the climate talks for the second year running – has encouraged policies maximising oil, gas, and coal production to address the disruptions.

South Korea, India, Thailand and other Asian nations have increased their reliance on coal or taken steps to boost coal-fired power generation.

“A lot of people who previously might have been embarrassed to argue for continuing very high use of fossil fuel are now feeling empowered to make that case,” said John Holdren of Harvard University, who was a science adviser to Barack Obama when he was US president.

news.title: Trump Rules Out Amnesty In Any Immigration Deal With Democrats
news.text: After suggesting he was open to negotiating a deal with Democrats on an immigration policy that he described as too tough, President Donald Trump on Monday defended his administration's deportation policy and said he was opposed to any immigration deal that would include "amnesty" for immigrants living in the US illegally. The comments from Trump came after Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin earlier Monday also said while he has been fielding calls from Democrats interested in working on immigration policy, he was adamantly opposed to any deal that would include amnesty. The midterm elections highlighted voters' disaffection toward the administration's hard-line immigration enforcement activities. But the comments from both Trump and Mullin reflected the mixed messaging from the administration in the aftermath of the election and emphasised how complicated it will be for a new Congress controlled by Democrats to find any common ground when it comes to the issue of immigration. Immigration has long been one of the most intractable issues facing Congress, with any deal that gives people in the country illegally a pathway to resolve their status often characterised by anti-immigration critics as amnesty. But advocates have said that longtime immigrants who've lived in the US for years and worked and raised families here deserve a way to come out of the shadows and legalise their status. "There won't be amnesty," Trump told reporters at the White House. "Somebody suggested, will there be amnesty? No, but - they came in. They knew the law." Trump defended his administration's deportation policy as "very strong." Asked if he had spoken with Stephen Miller, his newly promoted chief of staff who was the architect of his immigration crackdown, about immigration changes, Trump said no."My policy hasn't changed," he said, adding that the focus will be on removing "the worst of the worst." In comparison, during an interview that aired Sunday with "60 Minutes," Trump said "killers" and "drug dealers" in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay "if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes."Trump rode back into power with a promise to crack down on immigration. During the first two years of his second term, arrests of immigrants surged, including through high-profile operations in large US cities that sometimes turned violent. And voters appeared to disapprove of the tactics. Nationally, about six in 10 voters said the Trump administration's actions on immigration enforcement had "gone too far," according to The AP Voter Poll, a survey of more than 100,000 midterm voters. A similar share disapproved of how Immigration and Customs Enforcement was doing its job. Mullin earlier Monday reiterated Trump's willingness to work with Democrats on the issue, although he said that he and the president haven't yet discussed any concrete immigration policy changes in the aftermath of the midterm elections. Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of a conference near Washington DC, Mullin also said he is strongly opposed to any amnesty for people living in the US illegally. Mullin, who was a senator and House representative before becoming Trump's Homeland Security secretary earlier this year, said after the election he's been fielding calls from Democrats that he worked with in Congress on bipartisan issues."I've let the president know that those calls are coming in. And the president has said, you know, let's start working with them and then let's meet at some point. So that's the extent of the conversation," Mullin said.  UFC chief declines Trump’s White House job offer 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) chief Dana White turned down President Donald Trump’s — apparently jovial — offer of a job as press secretary in a surprise appearance at the White House on Monday.

Trump stunned the world by saying on social media on Saturday that he had asked White to take on the high-profile post — but a day later the 80-year-old president said he was “only kidding.”

The 57-year-old cage fighting boss visited the White House on Monday, and Trump brought him out for a chaotic news conference in the James Brady Briefing Room.

“So let me ask you the big question. Would you like to be press secretary of the United States of America? Or do you just want to stay with this ridiculous UFC? Huh?” Trump said.

“Thank you for the offer, sir — for the offer, I have no, no — I do not want to be in politics,” White replied.

Trump smiled and headed out of the room, saying: “I am devastated to hear this. Goodbye, everybody.”

The press secretary’s post has been been vacant since Katie Zacharia left on October 16 after less than a week in the post. Her combative predecessor Karoline Leavitt left in August after a year and a half in the job.

Trump’s announcement that he had offered the high-profile job to “violent Fighter and Warrior” White had sparked speculation that he was ready for a aggressive stance after the Republican Party’s stunning midterm elections defeat.

White is a long-time friend of the president and helped host a massive UFC match on the White House lawn earlier this year.

But there was also some skepticism about the president’s announcement, and Trump said Sunday night that he had been joking.

– ‘Beat the hell out of you’ –

Leading out White to the podium on Monday, Trump said he had been “having a little fun.”

“He’s a great guy,” Trump told the room full of reporters. “The only problem is he’ll talk for a little while and then he’s going to beat the hell out of you.”

Standing at the lectern and wearing a black t-shirt and jacket, White looked like he might be more comfortable in the octagon — the ring used for UFC fights.

“I’ve always wanted to do this. Who has the first question?” he joked — before quickliy adding: “I have zero political aspirations.”

White added that “the last 24 hours of my life has been insane” since Trump made the announcement.

Asked by a journalist to confirm he had said no to the job, White added: “I don’t tell the president ‘no’ to anything… I didn’t want to be disrespectful and say anything until he said something first.”

Trump then took a series of questions on more weighty matters, from the Iran and Ukraine wars to the possible impeachment of Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth and a spy scandal engulfing Nvidia boss Jensen Huang.

news.title: Asian stocks gain as Wall Street tech rally lifts investor sentiment
news.text: Hong Kong Asian stocks advanced Tuesday after US stocks rallied, recovering most of their big losses from last week. US futures edged higher, and oil prices fell. Japan's benchmark Nikkei 225 rose 2.6 per cent to 60,279.37. Shares in OpenAI investor SoftBank Group jumped 15 per cent ahead of the company's earnings release later in the day. Its share price had fallen to its lowest level in a year on Monday. Computer chip equipment maker Tokyo Electron surged 5.6 per cent, and testing equipment maker Advantest gained 3.4 per cent. South Korea's Kospi climbed 4 per cent to 5,219.37. Chipmakers Samsung Electronics gained 4.6 per cent, and SK Hynix climbed 5.6 per cent. In Hong Kong, the Hang Seng rose 0.4 per cent to 24,535.74, while the Shanghai Composite index edged 0.4 per cent higher to 3,673.54. China's exports in October climbed 35.2 per cent from a year earlier, while imports grew 41.6 per cent, according to customs data released on Tuesday. That has put the country on track for another record for the year since the trade surplus for 2026 has already surpassed USD 1 trillion. Australia's S&P/ASX 200 rose 1.1 per cent to 9,131.70. Markets closed today for Diwali-Balipratipada, trading to resume on November 11 Markets closed today for Diwali-Balipratipada, trading to resume on November 11 n the previous trading session on Monday, the benchmark BSE Sensex gained 0.13% to close at 81,106.65, while the broader NSE Nifty 50 advanced 0.23% to 25,044.65 Markets closed today for Diwali-Balipratipada, trading to resume on November 11 Taiwan's Taiex advanced 3.4 per cent. On Monday, the S&P 500 jumped 2.3 per cent for a second straight gain after a wipeout on worries that Democratic victories in the US midterm elections could lead to a slowdown in the construction of AI data centres. The best day for the index since April has it sitting just 3.4 per cent below its all-time high set last month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 2.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite rose 2.7 per cent. Stocks were lifted by a decline in the price of Brent crude. It fell after President Donald Trump told CNN over the weekend that a resumption of strikes on Iran is “highly unlikely” if the United States sees progress in negotiations toward ending the war. However, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that Iranian demands had sometimes been “outrageous and ridiculous.” Several strong profit reports from big US companies also helped buoy shares. Constellation Energy climbed 10.5 per cent after the power company reported both profit and revenue for the summer that topped analysts' expectations. Those data centres are coming under increased scrutiny following Democratic victories in last week's election. The worry is that governments could impose restrictions on the industry, which would mean fewer purchases of artificial-intelligence-related products and services around the AI boom. That was on top of concerns that new construction of AI data centres may slow because of how expensive it's become to borrow money. Before that, critics were already saying AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble. The stock that has become the face of the AI boom, Nvidia, fell 4.3 per cent. The chip company said it's investigating after its CEO, Jensen Huang, acknowledged an intimate relationship with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, US intelligence determined was gathering information for China. Nvidia's board said it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, but its inquiry would examine all available information. Guo Jiakun, spokesperson for China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs, called the allegations “nothing but smears against China.” The pullback in Treasury yields over the last month has helped rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans to ease. It also gave a boost to prices for stocks and other investments. In other dealings early Tuesday, the price of Brent crude, the international standard, edged 0.9 per cent lower to USD 91.74 a barrel. US benchmark crude oil fell 1 per cent to USD 85.97 per barrel. The US dollar rose to 158.06 Japanese yen from 157.90 yen. The euro fell to USD 1.1222 from USD 1.1266. (AP) SKS SKS

news.title: What happens after a midterm tsunami? Lessons from 1974 and 1994
news.text: Virginia There were lots of surprises on the evening of Nov. 3 when the picture of the Democratic midterm success began to be painted on network news touch screens. The maps kept getting bluer. Eventually, it was clear that this was not an ordinary midterm cycle when the party out of power slaps the wrist of the sitting president and his administration. It was much bigger than that, something on a scale the U.S. has seen only two times in the past half-century. One was the Newt Gingrich “revolution” in 1994 that put Republicans in control of the House of Representatives for the first time in 40 years. The other was the election of 1974 that flooded Capitol Hill with “Watergate babies” – new members elected just after the Nixon-era scandals. In both cases there were high hopes that big changes would take place in the aftermath of remarkable midterm elections. The actual results were more modest than the victors expected. 1994’s wipeout election The 1994 midterm elections gave the Republican Party a dramatic victory. The Democrats lost their majority in the Senate, and 54 seats were flipped in the House of Representatives, making Gingrich the first Republican speaker of the House since Eisenhower lived in the White House. It was a wipeout election that had not been expected, and it changed the dynamics of Democrat Bill Clinton’s presidency. The combative Gingrich emerged as a political celebrity; partisanship intensified and gridlock became the new norm. Confrontations over spending led to controversial government shutdowns and the first modern threat to default on America’s debt obligations. Because the new Republican congressional majorities appeared to overreach in their efforts to cut taxes and spending, Clinton was able to recover sufficient popularity to win a second term. In the run-up to his bid for reelection, Clinton took the electoral rebuke of 1994 to heart and followed a centrist strategy that represented a move to the right of longtime Democratic positions on welfare, crime and immigration. He continued to oppose many Republican policy proposals but worked with Republicans to craft welfare reform legislation and new bills dealing with crime and immigration. Budget confrontation eventually gave way to compromise, and for a few years in the late 1990s the United States had a balanced budget. Partisanship became more personal in Clinton’s second term when Gingrich pushed for impeachment following the revelations of the president’s affair with Monica Lewinsky. Clinton, with a tarnished reputation, survived his Senate trial. Ironically, it was Gingrich who resigned after failing to remove the president at the ballot box or in the impeachment process. Gingrich, the biggest winner in the 1994 midterms, left office with a promised revolution largely unrealized. 1974’s Watergate reformers Going back even further in American political history, the midterm elections following President Richard Nixon’s resignation after the Watergate scandal produced a Democratic Party victory. That victory was not a surprise; the scale of it was. Democrats, who already had majorities in the House and Senate, won a huge margin in the congressional popular vote and brought new members to both chambers who were younger, more liberal and reform-minded. They wanted to prevent future Watergates. New laws would make the government more open, more honest and more accountable. New and more staff would allow Congress to be less reliant on executive branch information and better able to act in foreign policy and budget management. Special prosecutors would be appointed to investigate abuses of power and violations of law. A Democrat, Jimmy Carter, would be elected president two years after the massive 1974 midterm victory, and more reform legislation would be passed. The post-Watergate congressional agenda was long and bold – the war powers resolution, a freedom of information act, the creation of inspectors general, campaign finance reform, a presidential records act and new legislation to regulate foreign intelligence surveillance and the bribing of foreign officials. These new laws were supposed to stop, or uncover, the kind of wrongdoing that made Nixon an imperial president. The new laws and institutions certainly made a difference – but not without creating their own problems. All the post-Watergate presidents thought the war powers resolution was unconstitutional, objecting to its restrictions on the president’s authority as commander in chief, and US military interventions overseas continued to occur. Special prosecutors conducted many investigations, but often at great expense and without adequate supervision or meaningful results. Carter, narrowly elected president in 1976, served only one term and lost reelection to Ronald Reagan, who fully restored the Republican Party’s dominance in presidential politics. Over time, many presidents, especially Donald Trump, dismantled or ignored important elements of the post-Watergate reforms. The large and enthusiastic congressional majorities that took power after the 1974 midterms were energetic but produced a political legacy with complicated and controversial results. Chaos and conflict – or compromise? What is the country likely to see in the next few months and the next two years? Will it be chaos, conflict and occasional compromise, like the politics that followed the midterms in 1994? Or will it be earnest and sometimes heavy-handed congressional efforts to investigate and prevent presidential wrongdoing, like those that swept through Washington after 1974? Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant.
news.summary: Surprising midterm elections that create new majorities on Capitol Hill look to be revolutions in the days after they occur. Years later, they often appear to be more complex – and less significant

news.title: Past talks involving Russia and Ukraine have yielded little progress toward peace
news.text:
Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, in the latest bid to end the war.

Key developments from past sessions since Moscow's full-scale invasion of its neighbor on Feb. 24, 2022:

Feb. 28, 2022: Ukrainian and Russian delegations meet in neighboring Belarus for the first time after the invasion. Talks continue for two weeks, deciding only on humanitarian corridors for evacuating civilians.

March 10, 2022: Russian and Ukrainian Foreign Ministers Sergey Lavrov and Dmytro Kuleba meet in Antalya, Turkey.

March 21, 2022: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy calls for direct talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, an idea rebuffed by Lavrov. 

March 28-30, 2022: Delegations meet in Istanbul to work on a draft peace agreement. Moscow says it's willing to “fundamentally cut back” military activity near Kyiv and the northern city of Chernihiv; Ukraine says it's open to discussing neutral status for Ukraine if its security is backed by other nations.

April 7, 2022: Lavrov rejects a Ukrainian proposal as “unacceptable," saying Kyiv has walked back on an agreement to exempt the Crimean Peninsula from wider Ukrainian security guarantees. Russia illegally annexed Crimea in 2014.

April 26, 2022: U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres visits Russia to discuss ending the war.

May 13, 2022: U.S. Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin calls his Russian counterpart, their first contact since war began.

July 22, 2022: Russia and Ukraine, with mediation by Turkey and the U.N., agree to unblock grain supplies stuck in Ukraine’s Black Sea ports. Russia withdraws from the deal a year later.

Sept. 30, 2022: Russia illegally annexes the Ukrainian regions of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, even though it doesn’t fully control any of them. Ukraine responds by applying to join NATO and by enacting a decree that declares negotiations with Putin “impossible.”

Nov. 15, 2022: Zelenskyy unveils a 10-point peace plan at the G20 summit in Indonesia.

June 16-17, 2023: African leaders travel to Kyiv and St. Petersburg on a peace mission, without success.

June 25, 2023: Officials from 15 countries, including the U.S., India, Brazil, South Africa, Saudi Arabia, Turkey and several representatives from the European Union, meet in Copenhagen, Denmark, to discuss Zelenskyy’s peace plan.

Aug. 5-6, 2023: Two days of discussions on the war begin in Saudi Arabia with delegates from 40 countries, including China, India, South Africa and Brazil, but not Russia. No joint statements are issued.

Oct. 28-29, 2023: Delegates from 65 countries meet in Malta to continue talks on Zelenskyy’s peace plan. Russia, which dismissed the talks, was not invited. China, though invited, did not participate.

June 15-16, 2024: Representatives of 92 nations meet in Nidwalden, Switzerland, to discuss Ukraine’s peace plan, but a consensus remains elusive. The summit’s final statement is backed by most — but not all — participants.

Dec. 7, 2024: U.S. President-elect Donald Trump travels to Paris and meets Zelenskyy and other European leaders.

Feb. 12, 2025: Trump and Putin speak directly via telephone and agree to begin negotiations on ending the war. The conversation ends a three-year U.S.-led effort to isolate Putin.

Feb. 18, 2025: Russian and U.S. officials, including Lavrov and U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meet in Saudi Arabia and agree to work toward ending the war, as well as restoring bilateral ties. Ukrainian officials are not invited.

Feb. 28, 2025: Zelenskyy holds a contentious meeting with Trump, Rubio and Vice President JD Vance in the White House. A proposed minerals deal between the countries is left unsigned.

March 11, 2025: U.S. and Ukrainian officials meet in Saudi Arabia, with Americans proposing a plan for a 30-day ceasefire. Kyiv agrees to the proposed truce. 

March 13, 2025: Putin effectively rejects the ceasefire plan, stating certain issues still must be resolved. He also meets with U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff in Moscow. Witkoff travels to Russia twice more in April to meet Putin.

March 23-24, 2025: The U.S. holds separate talks with each side in Saudi Arabia. The White House says they agreed to a Black Sea truce. 

May 16, 2025: Russia and Ukraine meet directly in Istanbul, under Turkish mediation, for the first time in three years and agree to swap 1,000 prisoners from each side. Ukraine's delegation was led by Defense Minister Rustem Umerov, while Russia's was headed by Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky.

June 2 and July 23, 2025: Two more rounds of talks between Russia and Ukraine in Istanbul produce an exchange of draft memorandums.

Aug. 15, 2025: Trump and Putin meet in Anchorage, Alaska. The summit produces no concrete peace agreement, ceasefire deal, or specific resolution on the war in Ukraine. International observers widely view it as a symbolic boost for Moscow. 

Aug. 18, 2025: Trump hosts Zelenskyy and European leaders at the White House. Discussions center on establishing robust security guarantees for Ukraine.

November 2025: A 28-point U.S.-Russian peace plan emerges, and critics say it favors Moscow. On Nov. 23, it's cut to 19 points during discussions involving Washington, Kyiv and Ukraine’s European allies in Geneva.

Dec. 2, 2025: Putin, his adviser Yuri Ushakov and Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev meet Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner in Moscow. Ushakov describes the meeting as constructive but says much work remains.

Dec. 4-6, 2025: Witkoff and Kushner meet a Ukrainian delegation headed by Umerov and Chief of General Staff Gen. Andriy Hnatov in Miami.

Dec. 14-15, 2025: Ukrainian officials, including Zelenskyy, travel to Berlin for talks with Witkoff and Kushner. U.S. officials say Washington agrees to provide Kyiv with unspecified security guarantees.

Dec. 20-21, 2025: Dmitriev holds talks with Witkoff and Kushner in Miami. The Americans meet separately with a Ukrainian delegation.

Dec. 28, 2025: Zelenskyy meets in Florida with Trump, who calls Putin beforehand.

Jan. 6-7, 2026: Zelenskyy and other Ukrainians attend a summit of the “Coalition of the Willing” in Paris and hold talks with Witkoff and Kushner. Kyiv’s allies tout major progress for defending Ukraine if a peace deal is struck, saying they were ready to provide international guarantees to deter Russia from attacking again.

Jan. 17, 2026: A Ukrainian delegation arrives in the U.S. for talks.

Jan. 20-22, 2026: Witkoff and Kushner meet separately in Davos, Switzerland, with Ukrainian and Russian delegations. Zelenskyy then meets Trump for what the U.S. leader calls “very good” talks. Zelenskyy calls them “productive and meaningful.”

Jan. 23-24, 2026: Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. delegates meet in Abu Dhabi in the first known instance of Trump administration officials sitting down with both countries to try to halt the war.

Feb. 4-5, 2026: A second round of trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi leads to swapping 157 prisoners from each side.

Feb. 17-18, 2026: The third round of trilateral negotiations in Geneva, Switzerland, ends without a breakthrough.

Feb. 28, 2026: The U.S. and Israel begin a war with Iran, leading the Trump administration to wind down talks with Russian and Ukrainian officials.

May 7, 2026: Umerov meets in Miami with U.S. officials, as negotiations remain stalled.

Sept. 5-6, 2026: Witkoff and Kushner meet Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5, and in Kyiv with Zelenskyy the next day. 

Oct. 21, 2026: Ushakov says Putin agrees “in principle” with Witkoff to resume talks after Nov. 10. 

Oct. 27-Nov. 1, 2026: After intervention by U.S. first lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, a localized ceasefire is reached for the region around the Russia-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine to allow the evacuation of some of its residents and the delivery of food and other supplies.
news.summary: Negotiators from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington are scheduled to meet in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates, on Tuesday and Wednesday for talks aimed at trying to end Russia's 4 1/2-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine

news.title: India speaks with Russia, Ukraine ahead of US-led peace talks
news.text:
India held high-level discussions with Russia and Ukraine as New Delhi seeks a more active role in efforts to end their war, ahead of a new round of US-brokered peace talks set to start Tuesday.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi spoke by telephone Monday with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and expressed willingness to contribute to efforts to peacefully end the conflict, according to a statement from India’s government. India for years has taken a cautious approach to the conflict, in part because of its longstanding ties with Russia, but has recently stepped up its diplomacy with Moscow and Kyiv.

Zelenskyy said in a post on X that India is ready to mediate on establishing food corridors amid what he described as Russia’s blocking of grain exports through the Black Sea.

Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar separately spoke by phone on Monday with Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov to discuss international matters as well as bilateral issues, according to a Russian Foreign Ministry statement.

Russian and Ukrainian envoys at the planned US-mediated meeting in Abu Dhabi will discuss territorial issues and proposals for ceasefire monitoring, according to a senior US official. The meeting will resume talks put on hold in February when the Trump administration’s focus shifted to the Iran war.

Russia is sending a higher-level team than in previous rounds of similar talks, suggesting greater openness to substantive negotiations after months of diplomatic deadlock.

India’s diplomacy on the Russia-Ukraine conflict began after attacks in July killed and injured Indian sailors, prompting New Delhi to raise the issue with Moscow and Kyiv, Jaishankar said in October at the Kautilya Economic Conclave in New Delhi.

India has called for a halt to the fighting but has been reluctant to criticize the Kremlin, abstaining from United Nations votes condemning the war. Modi called on Russian President Vladimir Putin to end the conflict during a meeting on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization summit in Kyrgyzstan in late August.

Relations between Moscow and New Delhi date back decades to the Cold War, when the Soviet Union provided military backing and arms to a then-nonaligned India while Washington was closely tied to neighboring Pakistan.

When Modi met Putin on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in September, the two pledged to deepen ties, underscoring their close relationship even as Washington pressed New Delhi to distance itself from Moscow.

Putin agreed to resume trilateral negotiations with the US and Ukraine on a potential peace deal when he met President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff in Moscow in October. 

The US has sought to use its position as India’s top trading partner to pressure New Delhi to stop buying Russian oil. India’s purchases initially declined before picking up again during the Middle East war.

The renewed diplomatic push follows a sharp escalation in long-range attacks. Russia has launched repeated missile and drone barrages against Kyiv and other major Ukrainian cities, with strikes on energy, transport and other infrastructure adding to pressure on civilians as winter approaches.

news.title: Nvidia loses $1.57 trillion in market value amid AI growth fears and CEO probe
news.text: Digital Desk | New Delhi, Nov 10 (IANS) US chipmaker Nvidia has lost around $1.57 trillion in market capitalisation after its shares plunged more than 26 per cent from their 52-week high with entering bear-market territory amid investor concerns over artificial intelligence (AI) spending and growing scrutiny surrounding its Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang. The company's market capitalisation stood at $4.31 trillion at the close of trading on November 9, down from approximately $5.88 trillion when its shares touched a 52-week high of $243.37, according to a report by NDTV Profit. Moreover, the estimated erosion in market value is larger than the entire market capitalisation of electric vehicle manufacturer Tesla, which stands at around $1.49 trillion. Nvidia shares closed at $178.67 on November 9, a decline of around 26.6 per cent from their 52-week peak. The stock has also witnessed sustained selling pressure, falling 14 per cent over the past week and 22 per cent over the last 30 days. It has declined 18 per cent over three months and 17 per cent over six months. The sharp correction comes ahead of the company's quarterly earnings announcement scheduled for November 17 with investors closely monitoring the sustainability of global AI infrastructure spending and demand for advanced semiconductor chips. Adding to the company's challenges, recent developments involving Huang have brought the chipmaker's leadership under increased scrutiny. As per reports, Huang had engaged crisis communications firm Heller Inc. as early as October 2025, months before publicly acknowledging an extramarital relationship with a former executive of Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed. The communications firm was also brought into Nvidia's media response process following questions raised over the company's chip sales and possible diversion of advanced semiconductors to Chinese entities in violation of US export restrictions, they added. Moreover, Megaspeed had reportedly acquired nearly $2 billion worth of Nvidia chips, the report said. In a statement released on Sunday, Jensen Huang acknowledged having an affair with a former Megaspeed executive, without naming the woman. He also apologised to his family and Nvidia employees. Separately, Nvidia's board announced an independent investigation following reports that Huang had been targeted in a foreign intelligence operation. The board said it had no reason to believe that national security or confidential company information had been compromised. US President Donald Trump on Monday said the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) was looking into Huang's relationship with the woman suspected of having links to Chinese intelligence, while expressing confidence in the Nvidia chief. Trump said he had spoken to Huang earlier in the day and described him as a "very honourable man". "I know the FBI is looking into it, in terms of something else, and I think that he'll be in good shape," Trump told reporters at the White House. Investors are now awaiting Nvidia's upcoming earnings announcement for indications of future revenue growth, demand for AI processors and the pace of spending by major technology companies.
