news.title: US-brokered talks are set to start in Abu Dhabi to discuss Ukraine-Russia peace deal
news.text:
The three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States start Tuesday in the United Arab Emirates, renewing a push for peace after several rounds of negotiations earlier this year.

The two-day session in Abu Dhabi, the first such meeting since February, will focus on security guarantees. U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner said on X that he and fellow envoy Steve Witkoff were working on a "negotiated solution that can deliver lasting peace and create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment.”

 Russia and Ukraine hold to their divergent demands 

Moscow and Kyiv remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal to end the full-scale war, now nearing its five-year mark.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — the four regions that Moscow illegally annexed in September 2022 but never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO, accept strict limits on its military and drop restrictions on the Russian language and the Moscow-affiliated Orthodox Church in Ukraine.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won’t agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles. He has warned that Russia will achieve its goals by force if Kyiv refuses to meet its conditions for peace.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory that Russia has not been able to take on the battlefield. Zelenskyy also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues that an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled.

 Russia and Ukraine send experienced negotiators 

The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.

Russia’s chief negotiator is Putin aide Vladimir Medinsky, who has led Moscow’s team since the first direct peace talks with Ukraine in Istanbul, Turkey, in March 2022. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov and deputy chief of the General Staff’s operational department Yuri Zhigarlovsky.

Ukraine’s delegation is led by Rustem Umerov, head of the country’s Foreign Intelligence Service, who also attended earlier talks. It also reportedly includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, his deputy Sergiy Kyslytsya and Davyd Arakhamia, the parliamentary faction leader of Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party.

 The US says a broader European security deal is in the works 

Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.”

Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.” The discussions in Abu Dhabi will set the stage for “that engagement to begin in the near future, as part of a broader multilateral process,” he added.

Moscow has praised the broad approach.

“We can only welcome the (U.S.) negotiators on President Donald Trump’s request proposing to put the issue of collective security on top of the agenda of the talks on a Ukrainian settlement,” Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said.

Just before Moscow launched the all-out invasion in 2022, it demanded that NATO roll back its deployments in the alliance’s member countries in Central and Eastern Europe, seeing their presence as a security threat. Similar demands will likely be part of any comprehensive peace deal proposed by Russia.

Kushner said that before the start of the three-way talks, he and Witkoff will meet separately with envoys from Ukraine, the European Union, NATO, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Italy to “continue the close consultation and coordination we have undertaken on European security and Ukraine’s postwar future over the past several weeks.”

Some in the EU see Washington's proposals as too accommodating to Moscow. 

Moscow has objected to the Europeans’ involvement in the three-way talks but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.

 Russia and Ukraine have escalated aerial attacks 

While the ground battles have morphed into a war of attrition along the 1,200-kilometer (about 750-mile) front line, Russia and Ukraine have ramped up their long-range strikes with drones and missiles.

Russia has intensified its air campaign against Ukraine’s power grid, seeking to weaken the country’s resolve as winter sets in. Moscow has relied on ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, taking advantage of Ukraine’s shortage of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors.

Ukraine, meanwhile, has escalated its drone strikes on Russian oil refineries.
news.summary: Three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are set to start in the United Arab Emirates, renewing a push for peace after several rounds of negotiations earlier this year

news.title: Dana White reveals phone call from Trump just moments after president claimed to have offered UFC boss press secretary job
news.text:
UFC chief Dana White has revealed that Donald Trump called him up just moments after jokingly offering the White House press secretary role. 

On Saturday afternoon, Trump took to Truth Social to announce that 'the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior' had been offered the job of press secretary. He then added a personal plea: 'Dana, please take the job!'

UFC boss White then admitted on Saturday night that, in the wake of Trump's bombshell offer, he was heading to Washington DC straight away.

Social media quickly descended into a frenzy as fans speculated whether White was genuinely about to accept the role offered by his longtime friend. 

However, White has now lifted the lid on the saga, explaining he was primarily flying to the nation's capital to secure the president's signature on a trading card.

In an interview with TMZ, White explained that trading card company Topps created a special 1-of-1 collectible commemorating the UFC Freedom 250 event held on the White House South Lawn in June.

'Me and the president wore patches that night for Freedom 250, and the cards are done so he's going to sign the card tonight. That's one of the reasons why I'm here,' White explained to TMZ.

When asked about the press secretary rumors, the fight promoter insisted he had nothing to do with the viral stunt and was completely caught off guard by the post.

'He put that out! The press secretary thing was him. Everyone has been blowing me up, asking me questions. I'm not going to be disrespectful and say anything. It's his thing!' White said.

Trump later clarified his shock job offer was simply a joke, but White revealed the president actually phoned him just moments after making the public declaration to give him a quick heads-up.

'Yeah, he called me,' White revealed, noting that he was already scheduled to travel to DC before the political rumor mill went completely into overdrive.

President Trump gave an impromptu press briefing on Monday afternoon alongside UFC CEO White. 

Pressed by CNN's Kaitlan Collins on whether he had accepted the post recently vacated by Katie Zacharia and Karoline Leavitt, White said he never tells the president 'no.' 

'I don't tell the president no to anything,' he responded. 'I didn't say no.'

Trump then shot back that he had jokingly announced White was press secretary last week after what he called 'a very bad press day.' 

'I think I'm going to get Dana White to be my new press secretary,' Trump recalled musing last week. 

Admitting he was 'sort of kidding' with the announcement, Trump noted the press ran with it and immediately 'wrote the stories.' Bringing White to the briefing room on Monday was just 'for a little fun,' Trump continued. 

But at the end of the briefing, White conceded he does not want the role nor any other job in politics.
news.summary: On Saturday afternoon, Trump took to Truth Social to announce that 'the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior' had been offered the job of press secretary.

news.title: A suspected spy, a high-profile affair and the billionaire tech bro at the heart of the Nvidia scandal
news.text:
Billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has admitted to having an affair with a woman suspected of being a spy feeding information to Beijing. 

The 63-year-old, currently ranked as the eighth richest man in the world by Forbes, has apologised for being unfaithful to his wife and said he takes “full responsibility” for his actions. 

Nvidia is reported to have sold nearly $5bn in AI chips to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based computing company where his lover Alice Huang previously worked as managing director. 

The board of his AI chipmaking company has now opened an independent investigation into reports that Huang has “been the target of a foreign intelligence effort”. 

It comes amid the ongoing rivalry between China and the US as they remain locked in a race for AI development.

Below, The Independent looks at the key players in the still-developing scandal. 

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, to be a spy working for the Chinese government.

Huang, who is no relation to the Nvidia CEO despite having the same name, is a former executive at the Singapore-based data centre and cloud computing firm, Megaspeed International. 

It is unclear when the pair’s affair began, but pictures of the two at a Taipei bar in 2024 have since been published in the New York Post. 

The New York Times reports that it was around this time that Megaspeed began a multibillion-dollar purchase of advanced AI microchips, which to many in the industry appeared to come out of nowhere. 

The pair was also seen leaving a Taipei restaurant in May 2025. In livestreams during this period, she can be seen wearing a pink dress and apparently kissing him on the cheek. 

According to AFP, online searches reveal Huang’s previous jobs include working at HSBC and as a journalist at Chinese media outlets CCTV and Hunan TV. However, the news agency notes it is unable to verify the information. 

The New York Times reported that a memo circulating among top policymakers last year cited intelligence that a Chinese businesswoman affiliated with Huang was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. 

The outlet said that Huang speaks good English and has connections at the highest levels of the AI industry. Megaspeed is reportedly building data centres in Southeast Asia and then renting this computing power to Chinese internet firm Alibaba, which is akin to the country’s Amazon. 

According to the Times, this has allowed China to purchase advanced Nvidia chips, whose sale to China is otherwise limited by the United States.

Nvidia said it had not been informed by US officials of the risk of Alice Huang being a spy. China, meanwhile, has strongly denied the claims of a spy plot. 

Liu Chang, a spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in Washington, told The New York Times that the claims were a campaign of “groundless smears and slanders” against Beijing. 

British shadow foreign secretary Tom Tugendhat said it is possible the Chinese state could have recruited Huang after the affair had already commenced. 

He speculated it would not be beyond the country’s government to “threaten sending Huang’s family to prison were she not to cooperate; now she was in a position to do so.”

Huang met his wife Lori Mills, 65, at Oregon State University where the pair studied electrical engineering. In the early 1980s, they were lab partners and grew closer over time before marrying in 1985. 

Lori won him over with her offer to study together every Sunday, and he promised that he would be a CEO by the age of 30, the billionaire said in a previous interview.

Huang co-founded Nvidia around eight years later. His wife has kept a low profile but occasionally attends public events with her husband. 

The couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation in 2007, whose assets are estimated to be worth more than $9bn due to the surging value of Nvidia shares. 

Stephen Witt, the author of a biography on Jensen Huang, Thinking Machine, told the BBC that “for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad.”

“He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways,” he said. “Both of his children work for Nvidia: Spencer and Maddison.”

The leather-jacketed billionaire is known for adopting a rockstar persona, spending time with fans and signing autographs for supporters. 

He has saved his company from bankruptcy multiple times with the belief that AI would one day become essential in the market. It now provides computing systems to several companies, powering video games and AI models such as ChatGPT. 

US president Donald Trump has referred to him as an “honourable guy” and described the situation as “complex”. 

Huang was one of a small group of people along with Tesla billionaire Elon Musk who attended a state dinner when Chinese president Xi Jinping visited Washington earlier this year. His company is now estimated to be worth around $4.5 trillion.
news.summary: Billionaire and Silicon Valley ‘rockstar’ Jensen Huang has admitted to being unfaithful to his college sweetheart wife Lori. His company Nvidia is now investigating reports he has been the target of foreign intelligence. Maira Butt reports

news.title: Iran's Seven Demands and the Dangerous Illusion of Peace
news.text:
There is something breathtaking about the audacity of Iran's clerical dictatorship. Having dragged the Middle East into a devastating conflict, threatened international shipping, and attacked its neighbors, Tehran has presented Washington with seven demands that must be met before negotiations can begin. These reportedly include lifting American sanctions, releasing frozen Iranian assets, and paying war reparations. The mullahs want to be rewarded before discussing the consequences of their own behavior.

The proposal, delivered through Qatar, comes at a dangerous moment. With America's midterm elections over, President Donald Trump has refused to rule out renewed military operations against Iran. Tehran threatens retaliation on an even greater scale. Diplomats are scrambling to prevent another explosion of violence across a region already exhausted by war.

Avoiding further bloodshed is essential. But confusing the temporary absence of fighting with durable peace would be a grave mistake. During my 15 years in the European Parliament, including five years as president of its Delegation for Relations with Iraq, I witnessed Tehran's interference in neighboring countries. The regime cultivated militias, infiltrated political institutions, and exploited instability while presenting itself as a responsible diplomatic partner. The current negotiations bear the hallmarks of that familiar strategy.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, has declared that the Strait of Hormuz will remain restricted until Washington fulfills Tehran's conditions. A regime that has weaponized one of the world's most important maritime passages is effectively demanding payment for restoring freedom of navigation.

Tehran has discovered a particularly cynical way of exploiting the crisis. It has announced exemptions for vessels from China, India, Iraq, and Qatar. Chinese and Indian ships may be charged transit fees, while Qatar receives free passage. India is expected to provide medicines, China offers political backing, and Qatar remains the principal diplomatic intermediary. This is no generous concession to international commerce. It is a calculated attempt to divide the international community, secure essential supplies, and extract political and financial advantages from a crisis of Tehran's own making.

China, which purchases most of Iran's exported oil, welcomes preferential treatment. India needs reliable access to Gulf energy. Qatar has substantial commercial interests in keeping maritime routes functioning. Iraq remains deeply exposed to Iranian influence. Such arrangements establish an appalling precedent. Freedom of navigation becomes a privilege granted by an authoritarian regime rather than a principle of international law.

Meanwhile, Rezaei has traveled to Moscow for discussions with Vladimir Putin, carrying a personal message, allegedly from the shadowy Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Tehran is seeking Russian diplomatic support while exploring closer energy cooperation and regional security arrangements. Putin, accustomed to using energy and military pressure as instruments of foreign policy, will hardly be troubled by his Iranian partners' methods.

But what would happen if Washington accepted Tehran's demands? Sanctions relief and the release of frozen assets would provide substantial financial breathing space. There is little reason to believe these resources would primarily improve the miserable circumstances of ordinary Iranians. The Revolutionary Guards, security apparatus, and regional proxies would compete for renewed funding. Hezbollah in Lebanon, Hamas in Gaza, the Houthis in Yemen, and militias across Iraq have demonstrated the destructive consequences of Iran's regional ambitions. Giving the regime fresh resources without enforceable restrictions risks rebuilding these destabilizing networks.

Even more alarming is the nuclear question. Washington insists that Iran's nuclear program must form part of initial negotiations. Tehran wants its demands satisfied first. If sanctions disappear before credible nuclear safeguards are established, the regime could gain the time, money, and opportunity to reconstruct capabilities damaged during the war. Any agreement would have to contain intrusive international inspections, independently verifiable restrictions, and effective mechanisms for responding to violations. Promises from Tehran are insufficient. The history of nuclear diplomacy with the Islamic Republic should have taught Western governments that lesson.

There is another issue almost entirely absent from these frantic diplomatic exchanges. What about the Iranian people? While foreign ministers discuss sanctions, shipping lanes, and security guarantees, millions of Iranians remain trapped under a dictatorship that answers demands for freedom with imprisonment, torture, and executions. Their aspirations appear secondary to the governments seeking accommodation with Tehran.

The Iranian people’s struggle for democratic change deserves recognition. Any lasting settlement must distinguish between protecting Iran as a nation and preserving the clerical establishment that rules through fear. The international community should support a peaceful, democratic transition determined by Iranians themselves, with free elections, equality before the law, and separation of religion and state. Replacing one dictatorship with another would perpetuate the tragedy.

Where, then, does Iran go from here? Trump faces an unenviable choice. Renewed military action could unleash another disastrous regional confrontation. Capitulation could rescue a weakened dictatorship and encourage further nuclear and regional adventurism. Alternatively, Washington and its allies should pursue a negotiated end to hostilities while insisting upon verifiable commitments, freedom of navigation through Hormuz, and meaningful nuclear restrictions. But such negotiated provisions have been tried before without success.

It is time for the West to realize that the survival of the clerical regime is not synonymous with stability. Tehran's seven demands are less a blueprint for peace than an attempt to turn military confrontation into political and economic advantage. The mullahs are gambling that fear of another war will persuade their adversaries to concede what years of diplomatic pressure failed to secure. Rewarding that gamble would be disastrous. Peace is desperately needed. But a settlement that restores the regime's finances, revives its nuclear ambitions, and abandons the Iranian people would merely prepare the ground for another catastrophe.

The West has tried appeasement and has tried war. Both have failed. Now surely the way forward is for Western nations to support the Iranian people and their bid to overthrow this evil theocratic dictatorship and replace it with a democratic republic. The Middle East has suffered enough from agreements that postpone the reckoning while leaving the causes of conflict untouched. This time, the objective must be something more enduring than another temporary reprieve for Tehran's rulers.

Struan Stevenson was a member of the European Parliament representing Scotland (1999-2014), president of the Parliament's Delegation for Relations with Iraq (2009-14), and chairman of the Friends of a Free Iran Intergroup (2004-14). He is an author and international lecturer on the Middle East.

news.title: Thomas Massie Weighs Career Prospects Amid Pete Hegseth Impeachment Push
news.text: U.S. Representative Thomas Massie, who is leaving Congress after losing his Republican primary earlier this year, has reintroduced eight articles of impeachment against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, with a House vote expected as early as this week. President Donald Trump publicly defended his Pentagon chief on Monday, while Massie warned that Hegseth could face even greater scrutiny under a Democratic-controlled Congress. “They stand by them until the day they don't,” Massie said on CNN’s The Source Monday. During the interview, Massie said he believed there was a “high probability” Hegseth would not remain in his position through the end of the year. “When the Democrats get control in January, they are not going to be as polite as I am,” he said. The impeachment effort could be among Massie's final major actions in Congress. The Kentucky Republican lost the primary to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein and will not return for the next Congress. As for what comes next, Massie said he is weighing several possibilities but has not made a decision. “When one door closes, another door opens. I found 10 doors that have opened, and my hardest problem is deciding what to do next,” he said at a Monday news conference. “I haven't ruled anything out, except coming back here,” he added, referring to Congress. Newsweek has reached out to Massie for further comment. Why Is There a Push to Impeach Pete Hegseth? Massie reintroduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth on Monday, accusing the defense secretary of violating laws and the Constitution through the Trump administration's military operations. Three of the articles accuse Hegseth of violating the War Powers Resolution through the administration's military campaign against Iran. Other articles accuse him of dismantling safeguards intended to minimize civilian casualties, overseeing extrajudicial killings during strikes on suspected drug-trafficking vessels in the Caribbean Sea and eastern Pacific Ocean, and using Pentagon authority to retaliate against Democratic Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona over constitutionally protected speech. The resolution also addresses U.S. military operations in Yemen and the operation to capture former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth has rejected the impeachment push, calling the articles a “sham" and likening the effort to previous ones against Trump. “Didn't work against President Trump, and it won't work with me,” he said in a video posted to X Thursday. Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell previously told Newsweek that the secretary was “100% committed” to leading the department until the end of Trump's term in office. Massie has argued that Hegseth had an independent responsibility to refuse unlawful orders. “It's true that the president is culpable by asking Hegseth to carry out these orders, but Hegseth should not carry out illegal orders, and that's why we're impeaching him,” Massie said at the Monday news conference. Could Pete Hegseth Be Impeached? Massie's resolution could receive a House vote as soon as Wednesday, although the timing depends on how Republican leadership handles the measure. Massie has urged House Speaker Mike Johnson to allow the full House to debate and vote on the impeachment charges rather than dismissing the resolution or sending it to committee, which Massie argues could effectively kill the effort. Johnson has opposed the push, saying that impeachment “in the middle of hostilities abroad would be a terrible, terrible look, a terrible thing for our allies and our enemies to see that,” Johnson said. Under House rules, Johnson must rule on whether Massie's resolution qualifies as a privileged measure before the chamber can consider it. If it does, lawmakers would have to take it up within two legislative days. Senate Majority Leader John Thune also questioned the timing of the effort, saying he was not sure why the House was considering it now. “We'll see what their ultimate decision is over there,” Thune said of the House. “We'll have to deal with it accordingly here.” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is expected to become speaker when Democrats take control in January, said Sunday he is a “hard yes” on the impeachment effort. Several other Democrats have also voiced support. The House can impeach Hegseth with a simple majority vote. If the resolution passes, the matter would move to the Senate, where a two-thirds majority of senators present would be required to convict and remove him from office. What Has Donald Trump Said About Pete Hegseth? Trump defended Hegseth on Monday, saying he will stand by the defense secretary despite Massie's impeachment effort. The president praised Hegseth's handling of U.S. military operations, saying he had “won two wars,” referring to operations in Venezuela and Iran. Trump described the Venezuelan operation as “flawless” and said Hegseth was “certainly winning” the war in Iran. Trump also said Iran would “love to make a deal.” Trump also attacked Massie, calling him a “stone-cold loser,” saying he is an “automatic no vote” against Republicans. “There's something wrong with him,” the president added. Hegseth is scheduled to hold a news conference at 8 a.m. ET Tuesday. Massie suggested on CNN that the timing of the appearance reflected concern within the administration about the allegations. “Because they're worried,” Massie said. “I think the vote will not happen until he's had his news conference. He's going to go out there and try to defend himself.” Massie added that Hegseth might try to convince people he is “likable,” but argued that was not the issue. “The question in an impeachment is, have you broken any laws and have you violated the Constitution? And I argue in eight instances he has,” Massie said. Massie's Career Massie will leave Congress in January after losing the Republican primary in May to Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL endorsed by Trump. Gallrein went on to defeat Democrat Melissa Strange in the November 3 general election, winning the seat. He will succeed Massie in January. Before entering Congress, Massie served as Lewis County judge executive in Kentucky. He studied electrical and mechanical engineering at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, where he developed tech that allowed people to interact with computers through touch. After graduating, Massie founded SensAble Technologies, which raised more than $32 million in venture capital, according to his congressional biography. Massie was first elected to represent Kentucky's 4th Congressional District in 2012. During his time in Congress, he served on the House Judiciary and Transportation and Infrastructure committees. He has represented the district for 14 years. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. news.summary: The Kentucky Republican is weighing his next move while pressing ahead with efforts to impeach the defense secretary.

news.title: N. Korea's nuclear recognition demand may hinder Trump-Kim summit: ex-U.S. official
news.text:
WASHINGTON - North Korea's apparent demand to be recognized as a nuclear power could complicate U.S. President Donald Trump's efforts to arrange another summit with leader Kim Jong-un, a former senior State Department official said Monday.

"I think my understanding, at least, is that the North Koreans have communicated to the United States that the only condition under which there could be consideration for a summit is if the United States accepted North Korea as a nuclear power," Kurt Campbell, former deputy secretary of state, said.

Campbell made the remarks during a press briefing hosted by the Asia Group to preview Trump's upcoming trip to Asia, including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila and the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China.

"Given the current circumstances, I think that would be almost impossible for President Trump to accept," Campbell said, noting that it could face opposition from both Republicans and Democrats in Congress. "I don't think the political circumstances make it likely for anything other than maybe just a handshake of sorts."

Campbell, chairman of the Washington-based strategic advisory firm, said that senior members of Trump's team had shown strong interest in reestablishing contact with North Korea during the presidential transition.

He also pointed to a subtle competition between Beijing and Moscow for influence over North Korea. "I think China's primary focus right now in North Korea is to ensure that as North Korea works with Russia, that China remains the dominant interlocutor," he said.

Trump has repeatedly expressed interest in engaging with Kim again, citing their "good" personal relationship, fueling speculation about a possible meeting during the president's planned visit to China this month.

The two leaders had three in-person meetings during Trump's first term: the first in Singapore in June 2018, the second in Hanoi in February 2019 and the third at the inter-Korean border village of Panmunjom.

Stephen Biegun, former U.S. special representative for North Korea, also expressed skepticism about the prospects of renewed diplomacy.

"All these conditions suggest to me that it will be very difficult to find a pathway to restart diplomacy with North Korea," Biegun said during a separate discussion hosted by the Stimson Center and the Sejong Institute.

Biegun suggested that both Trump and Kim may be willing to participate in what he called "performative summitry," but questioned what either side would gain from such a meeting. "It still begs the question, particularly from American interests, why would we want to do this."

He nonetheless argued that renewed engagement could help restore security and stability on the Korean Peninsula, while suggesting that Pyongyang might want to find a way to reduce its dependence on Russia and China.

news.title: Trump midterm backlash has lessons for Ireland
news.text: There was one message for the Irish Government to learn from the US midterm elections - affordability, affordability and affordability. That was the number one issue in the minds of the American people and it is exactly the same back here in Ireland. The harsh truth is people across the globe are under financial pressure and sick to the teeth of being screwed on price for food, energy and fuel. The US President Donald Trump decided to ignore the will of the people having been re-elected with a mandate to cut rising prices. Instead he made the cost of living worse with his stupid tariffs and war with Iran. So the voters decided they had enough and rightly gave him and his Make America Great Again Republican party a bloody nose at the polls. The result meant an electoral wipe-out for Trump and his party while the Democrats got rewarded with thumping majorities in both the House of Representatives and the Senate. The fallout is that the mad king Trump no longer has the power or the authority to do whatever he wants. He and his regime will also face a spate of damaging investigations that will result in resignations, possible impeachments and seriously negative publicity. Our Government here and especially its two leaders Taoiseach Micheal Martin and the Tánaiste Simon Harris would be wise to watch and learn from what has happened in America. The simple lesson is that you ignore the voters at your peril and that there will be significant repercussions for both them and their parties if they continue to do so. The fact is the ordinary working class people of Ireland are seriously hurting. They are being screwed in their pocket everywhere they go and the coalition is not doing enough to stop it. At a time when the State has never been so wealthy with surplus budgets etc the Government could be doing far more to help families. Take the soaring cost of home heating oil for example, this is one of the biggest worries for the vast majority of householders in this country. There is absolutely no reason why they can not abolish the carbon tax on home heating oil altogether and slash the 13.5 % VAT rate, never mind NORA, the National Oil Reserve Levy, until the war in the Middle East is over. The other big issue is the soaring cost of electricity and the Government's failure to stop the ESB, which taxpayers own, from consistently hiking up prices and screwing customers to the wall. This country now pays the highest electricity prices in the world while the ESB makes a profit of €700 to €800 million a year and is rising fast. The useless Minister for Energy Darragh O'Brien is like a rabbit stuck in the spotlights and has sat on his hands and done nothing about it. The same politician has allowed Transport Infrastructure Ireland to hike up the cost of motorway tolls yet again, blaming inflation when motorists and hauliers are under serious financial pressure. At the same time the public has watched in silent fury at the bosses and top executives of semi-state companies being rewarded with massive pay rises - up to €80,000 to € 90,000 in some cases - while families in general nationwide are struggling to pay their bills. It is no wonder that Fianna Fail and Fine Gael are languishing at rock bottom in the opinion polls because voters believe they are not doing enough to help them. Unless things change radically and the coalition government takes radical decisive action to make people's lives easier, there will be a savage day of reckoning come the next General Election. Micheal Martin is not a stupid man so he and his Minister would be wide to pay attention to what has happened across the Atlantic or the two main parties in Government could face a permanent wipe-out. I spend a lot of time in the United States and I could see this anti-Trump backlash coming. If you think food prices here are rising far too quickly, you can count your blessings that you are not living in America because they are paying at least 30% more for food than what we are and then we are 30% dearer than Spain for instance. This country produces a huge amount of food so you would think we should be cheaper than most other EU countries but that is not the case. Trump will now be a lame duck President so to speak for the remaining two years in office. Our Government has three years left to run so are they going to actually help us with our soaring family bills or not? The choice is theirs so let's hope they will intervene and do the right thing. Social Welfare is there to help those in need and should not be seen as a long term source of income. Unless you are medically unfit there is no excuse for somebody not working and receiving the dole or unemployment assistance as it is called now, for years on end as they sit at home and do nothing all day. I have always believed that people out of work should be made to work for their unemployed benefit after a year or so. If this means sweeping the streets, cutting the grass in our parks, emptying bins, so be it. Do something worthwhile on behalf of the State that pays you. So Simon Harris has a point about people who are long term unemployed. Where we disagree is that I would rather make them work for the State than actually cut their money in the forms of a penalty, which is what he is proposing. I think the Labour Party were extremely foolish to come out and defend the people who never want to work. Harris was talking about pensioners or those on disability benefit. We all know who the long term unemployed are because every village and every town in Ireland has families who never worked a day in their lives and social welfare is a way of life. There are often three generations of dossers. I can't say I am sorry that Man City have now lost three games in a row. The thought of the financial cheats winning the Premier League again this season did not sit well with me. There is of course a long way to go and if there is any fairness in the world they will be deducted points for their dodgy dealings in the next year. Over at Old Trafford Man Utd continue to give us great entertainment following their 4-4 draw with Aston Villa. Nobody can say this current United team doesn't give value for money. It is quite amusing looking at them in the relegation zone. Remembering the fallen We attended a remembrance service last Saturday in Drogheda at the war memorial for all those from the town who lost their lives in World War 1. It was a very poignant and moving ceremony and a reminder how lucky we are. Many of those who perished signed up and fought for the British Army at the time on the promise that Ireland would get home rule. Those who survived the trenches and managed to return home were often treated like second class citizens in the new Irish Free State and were wrongly perceived as traitors. Thankfully attitudes have now changed and those Irish men who died in the Great War are getting the recognition they deserve. Hot school meals a true gift One of the best things this government has done is the introduction of the hot school meals scheme especially in deprived and poverty ridden areas around the county. It means that thousands of young children who might not be fed at home are at least being fed by the State. There are no easy fixes to child poverty but this programme is a positive step in the right direction. My heart goes out to Mandy Kelly, the Dundalk woman who has been fighting for over four years to get her two sons back after they were abducted by their father while on a family holiday in his native Egypt. She has spent the past fortnight in Cairo and two attempts to rescue the children by local police implementing an Egyptian court order awarding her custody, failed. The Government must drive and put diplomatic pressure on the Egyptian authorities to do the right thing and make a serious and honest effort to find these children. The two boys are Irish citizens and should be sent home. There is an international arrest warrant out for their father. Mandy is rightly deeply frustrated at what is happening and just wants to be reunited with her sons. This country may be neutral but there is no doubt there are countries out there such as Russia, who are determined to cause as much damage and disruption to our way of life. That is why we as a nation are on red alert this week while all the leaders of the EU descend on Dublin for meetings during the Irish EU Presidency. The enemies of Europe want to bring chaos to our land so keep your eyes open and if you see anything sinister report it to the Gardai. There is absolutely no doubt that from a security point of view this country is a joke and we need to spend billions in the years ahead so we can defend ourselves. Neutrality means having a proper and fully equipped army and being truly independent from a military point of view. The far left here of course like People Before Profit would rather forget about defending our nation and divert every penny instead to pay for those who don't want to work and sponge off the State. I hope you are all stocked up with food, have cash in your house, in case every online system goes down from cyber attacks. news.title: Who is Jensen Huang? The Nvidia CEO who built today’s AI – but could fall after affair with ‘Chinese spy’
news.text:
He’s known as the rock star chief executive, renowned for his trademark leather jackets and unconventional approach to business. For a while, Jensen Huang’s persona was confined to tech conferences and Nvidia board meetings. But with the rise of AI – and his pivotal role at its forefront – Huang is now a frequent fixture on the global stage, appearing alongside world leaders and before crowds chanting his name, demanding selfies and autographs on their chests.

Today, Huang is on TV screens and front pages around the world after admitting to an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. It is an unexpected twist in an unusual story, which has taken him from an immigrant schoolboy in rural Kentucky, to a Silicon Valley superstar marred in scandal.

After emigrating from Taiwan at the age of five, Jen-Hsun Huang and his family spent four years in Thailand before a political crisis in the country forced his parents to send him and his older brother to live with their uncle in the United States. 

Shortly after arriving, his uncle mistakenly enrolled the Huang brothers in a rural Kentucky institution that he believed was a prestigious American boarding school. It turned out to be a strict disciplinary and reform environment for troubled children, where young Jen-Hsun, who now went by Jensen, was assigned to clean bathrooms and scrub toilets.

He spent two years there, before his parents arrived and removed him. But he credits that time to instilling in him a strong work ethic.

“I was the only kid cleaning bathrooms, that was a lot of bathrooms,” he recalled in a 2022 interview on Stratechery. “I think that we learned hard work, but it never occurred to us that it was hard work, we just thought that’s what kids do.”

The family settled in Portland, Oregon, where Huang graduated high school at just 16. With a keen interest in computers, he enrolled at Oregon State University and graduated in 1984 with a degree in electrical engineering. While studying there, he met his future wife, Lori Mills, with whom he now has two children.

His first job out of college was at Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), where he worked as a microprocessor designer for the semiconductor manufacturer. After a few years in the industry, he enrolled at Stanford University in California, where he earned a master’s degree in electrical engineering at the age of 29. Now in the heart of Silicon Valley, Huang and two fellow engineers had an idea that they believed could capitalise on the growing video games market. In a Denny’s restaurant in April 1993, Nvidia was born.

Along with Nvidia’s two other co-founders, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, Huang set about building specialised chips that could dramatically improve computer graphics. The company’s first major product was the NV1, a graphics card that launched in September 1995. Although technologically ambitious, it was ultimately unsuccessful due to its design approach being incompatible with the direction of the wider PC market.

The first commercial success came in 1997 with the RIVA 128, but it was not until 1999 that Nvidia made a big breakthrough with the GeForce 256, which it marketed as the world’s first GPU (graphics processing unit). The technology became a fundamental component of modern computers and helped usher in a new generation of video games.

It was in the early 2000s that Huang decided to pivot away from just a computer graphics company and decided to develop GPUs for general-purpose computing. The processor could be used for a huge variety of workloads, from weather modelling to medical research, but it was artificial intelligence that would turn Nvidia into a trillion-dollar company.

A decade before the arrival of ChatGPT, which kicked off the recent AI frenzy, Nvidia’s chips were being used by researchers to train neural networks and make breakthroughs in artificial intelligence. The increasingly powerful chips were at the forefront of pioneering developments in robotics, self-driving cars and data centres, making Nvidia perfectly placed for the next stage of the AI revolution. 

Huang had not necessarily predicted the emergence of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT, but the technology Nvidia had built made their development economically and technically possible.

Less than a year after the launch of ChatGPT, Nvidia’s market value crossed the $1 trillion mark. By 2025, it became the first publicly traded company to reach a market capitalisation of $4 trillion.

Its rise has seen Huang’s personal fortune rise above $150 billion, ranking him in the top 10 of the world’s wealthiest people, while also placing him at the centre of geopolitics.

As the head of a company whose chips have become one of the most sought-after resources in the global AI race, Huang holds regular meetings with world leaders and policy makers. He has attended state dinners at the White House for Chinese President Xi Jinping and speaks frequently with US President Donald Trump.

Huang has lobbied for the US to lift restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips overseas, which were put in place to prevent China from gaining an advantage in the AI space. His efforts have not been successful, as embargos remain, but the cheating scandal has raised sensitive questions.

The woman at the centre of the affair, Alice Huang, was an executive at Singapore-based data centre company MegaSpeed, an Nvidia customer that has faced allegations about diverting banned AI chips to China.

When asked about Huang’s affair, Trump described him as an “honorable guy” who “probably has an excuse for it”. Despite the president’s backing, the Nvidia boss is facing scrutiny from Congress over his relationship with a suspected intelligence operative.

He is also now the subject of an investigation from the company he founded and has led for more than 30 years. In a letter to employees on Sunday, Huang said that Nvidia’s board of directors had initiated an independent probe into potential national security concerns.

The outcome of these investigations could determine not just Huang’s future, but the direction of the entire global AI race.
news.summary: Immigrant schoolboy became a Silicon Valley superstar and billionaire by betting early on the chips that power today’s artificial intelligence, writes Anthony Cuthbertson. His vast power has led to one of technology’s biggest ever scandals – but could also protect him from it

The “Daily Show” editors then played another highlight from the interview, in which Trump tried to defend that “everyone’s” net worth has gone up in the last year-and-a-half, prompting Douthat to counter: “My net worth did not go up by $3 billion.”

“I think I’m going to enjoy this. I did not come into this interview thinking, ‘Uh, I’m going to enjoy this.’ But now, as I am watching this, I am thinking to myself, ‘I am going to enjoy this,’” Stewart said. “Let me prepare the table for the feast we are all about to enjoy. As regular viewers of our program know, Donald Trump has a somewhat high regard for his own financial acumen. In fact, not 20 minutes prior, in this very same interview we are watching, Donald Trump said this: ‘I’m really good at money and finances.’”

Stewart didn’t necessarily agree with this stance, quipping, “Best? Better than pool? Pool, renovation, finance and money? He’s better at money than pool.”

“My frustration with reporters is I wish someone would, like, hammer down on this,” Stewart continued. “Trump acts like he’s got all this money squirreled away in some index fund, and it just magically grew. Meanwhile, since the guy has returned to office, he’s made $125 million from foreign golf and real estate schemes, $117 million from legal settlements, $636 million from selling that bulls–t novelty meme coin. He’s gotten $800 million from his World Liberty Financial crypto company. Why can’t someone just bring this up to his face?”

Luckily for Stewart, Douthat did just that during the interview, confronting Trump over the fact that he’s a co-owner in his son’s cryptocurrency company.

“I think if I told you that story, and it was about the Biden family, if I said Joe Biden is the part-owner of a company and it has all of these investments from the Middle East, you would say that sounds corrupt,” Douthat said in the “60 Minutes” clip played on “The Daily Show.”

Stewart took a beat before responding, playfully making a series of delighted faces at the comment.

“I’ll have what he’s having,” he joked. “Woo! Oh my god! Ah! Man! First of all, I love that in the middle of that line of inquiry Trump is like, which– which son– which– which one of my sons runs this thing you brought [up]? Is it Lanky, Chinless, or New Guy? … And second of all, I love that Douthat is forcing Trump to compare himself to the Biden crime family.”

On Trump claiming in the interview that he knows “nothing about” his son’s business, Stewart erupted, “My god. Ross, you beautiful bearded bastard. Do you know what you’ve just done here? Do you have any idea what you just did here? You have made Donald Trump admit that the difference between him and Joe Biden is that Joe Biden is more aware of his surroundings. That’s what you did.”

A representative for the White House did not immediately respond to TheWrap’s request for comment.

news.title: PSX: stocks surge, KSE-100 up nearly 3,300 points
news.text:
Buying returned at the Pakistan Stock Exchange (PSX) after US President Donald Trump said US military action against Iran ​is not necessary “at this point”, with the benchmark KSE-100 gaining nearly 3,300 points during the opening minutes of trading on Tuesday.

At 9:45am, the benchmark index was hovering at 177,168.09, up 3,281.41 points or 1.89%.

Buying was observed in key sectors, including automobile assemblers, cement, commercial banks, oil and gas exploration companies, OMCs and power generation. Index-heavy stocks, including MARI, OGDC, PPL, PSO, HUBCO, HBL, MCB, MEBL and UBL, traded in the green.

The PSX recorded its strongest weekly rally in nearly six months, with the benchmark KSE-100 Index surging 7,477.44 points, or 4.5% week-on-week, to close at 173,886.69 points.

Globally, Asian stocks rose on Tuesday as a drop in oil prices after US President Donald Trump said he plans to hold off on new military strikes ​against Iran lifted sentiment ahead of US inflation data that could sway the near-term interest rate outlook.

Brent crude futures were hovering at their lowest ‌levels since early September, well below $100 per barrel, as investors pinned their hopes on possible talks between US and Iran.

They were last down 1% at $91.56 a barrel.

The US-Israeli war with Iran, which erupted at the end of February, has stoked inflationary concerns across the globe, spurring major central banks to raise rates in recent months.

Nick Twidale, chief market strategist at ATFX Global, said the latest ​developments offered hope that an end to the conflict could be approaching, but there was still a considerable gap between diplomacy and a lasting ​peace agreement.

The slump in oil prices eased inflation worries and helped lift stocks after last ​week’s rout as a sweeping victory by Democrats in the US midterm elections fed concerns that new regulations could dent the durability of the AI trade.

South Korea’s ​KOSPI rose over 5%, while Japan’s Nikkei gained about 3% in early trading. MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares pushed 1.5% higher, moving away from the seven-month low it hit last week.

On Monday, the S&P 500 clocked its biggest one-day jump since April, closing up 2.35% while the Nasdaq closed 2.7% higher, its best day in over four months.

Earnings ​reports due this week from tech companies including CoreWeave, a barometer of investor anxiety over AI, will be another test for markets as investors fret about the cost of the ‌AI buildout.

news.title: US stocks rally and recover most of last week's losses as oil prices swing lower
news.text: NEW YORK — The US stock market rallied Monday and recovered most of its big loss from last week as oil prices swung lower. The strength came even though Nvidia, one of Wall Street’s most influential stocks, sank.The S&P 500 jumped 2.3% for a second straight gain following a wipeout on worries that Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections could lead to a slowdown in the construction of AI data centers. The best day for the index since April has it sitting just 3.4% below its all-time high set last month.The Dow Jones Industrial Average leaped 1,104 points, or 2.2%, and the Nasdaq composite rose 2.7%.Stocks broadly got a lift from a 5.8% drop for the price of a barrel of Brent crude to $92.57. It’s been coming down from more than $112 at the start of the month amid uncertainty about what will happen with the war with Iran.The latest leg lower came after President Donald Trump told CNN over the weekend that a resumption of strikes is “highly unlikely” if the United States sees progress in negotiations, though U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that Iranian demands for ending the war had sometimes been “outrageous and ridiculous.”Several strong profit reports from big U.S. companies also helped lift the stock market.Constellation Energy climbed 10.5% after the power company reported both profit and revenue for the summer that topped analysts’ expectations. It’s been benefiting from deals announced recently to power data centers for Big Tech companies.Those data centers, and the blame they’re getting from voters for increases in power bills, are coming under increased scrutiny following Democratic victories in statehouses across the country in last week’s election. The worry is that governments could impose restrictions on the industry, which would mean fewer purchases of artificial-intelligence chips, electricity and other products and services around the AI boom.That built on top of worries already rattling the industry that further construction of AI data centers may slow because of how expensive it’s become to borrow money. Before that, even, critics were saying AI stock prices had shot too high and were in a bubble.Beyond power companies, other stocks linked to the AI build out also did better on Monday. Advanced Micro Devices rose 13.3% and recovered its 11% loss from last week. CoreWeave climbed 5.6% after tumbling 15.4% last week.That’s even though the stock that became the face of the AI boom, Nvidia, fell 4.3%. The chip company said it’s investigating its CEO, Jensen Huang, after he acknowledged an intimate relationship with a business executive who, according to The New York Times, U.S. intelligence determined was gathering information for China.Nvidia’s board said it has “no reason to believe” that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised but that its inquiry would examine all available information.Guo Jiakun, spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, called the allegations “nothing but smears against China.”All told, the S&P 500 rallied 173.08 points to 7,549.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped 1,104.02 to 52,389.75, and the Nasdaq composite leaped 673.71 to 25,253.14.In stock markets abroad, indexes rose across much of Europe and Asia. France's CAC 40 rose 1.2%, while Japan's Nikkei 225 jumped 2.3%. Indexes in China and South Korea were not as strong, and Seoul's Kospi fell 0.8%.In the bond market, Treasury yields held relatively steady following big moves last week. The yield on the 10-year Treasury inched up to 4.87% from 4.86% late Friday.It remains well below a peak above 5.30% that it reached last month, when it touched its highest level in two decades on worries about high inflation and the U.S. government’s big debt, among other things. The pullback in Treasury yields over the last month has helped rates for mortgages and other kinds of loans to ease. It also gave a boost to prices for stocks and other investments.

news.title: US-Mediated Talks Between Russia, Ukraine Begin Today In Abu Dhabi
news.text: Negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the United States will hold talks in Abu Dhabi Tuesday on ending Europe's worst conflict since World War II in the first such meeting in more than nine months, as another winter of war approaches.Europe -- alarmed by US President Donald Trump floating a deal with Moscow on European security ahead of the talks -- will also send representatives to Abu Dhabi. Trump has pushed for an end to the Russia-Ukraine war since returning to power, but previous talks produced no breakthroughs and the process became sidelined by the US-Israeli war against Iran. Europe and Ukraine fear the United States will force a deal on Kyiv that would amount to a de-facto capitulation, with Trump appearing to pivot towards Moscow this year.Moscow's invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands, displaced millions and has dragged on for 56 months, with the Kremlin showing no sign of backing down.Trump hinted Ukraine will have to give up land ahead of the talks, saying: "They're going to end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine."Russia occupies large swathes of Ukraine but, while its troops have grinded westwards, they have not been able to seize the whole of the Donetsk region. Moscow demands Kyiv surrender the parts of the region it still controls, vowing it will otherwise press on with its offensive. Ukraine -- which for more than 4.5 years has resisted a far larger invading army at a huge human cost -- has ruled out such a withdrawal. Russia pummelled Ukraine in the run-up to the talks and carried out one of its deadliest strikes yet -- with Kyiv saying 55 people were killed in a frontline village as they queued for humanitarian aid. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the intensified strikes were part of Moscow's strategy of "putting pressure on Ukraine's position" at the negotiations. Russia's Vladimir Putin, who launched the war in February 2022, has repeatedly refused broader ceasefire offers and face-to-face talks with Zelensky. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and special envoy Steve Witkoff will gather the enemy sides in Abu Dhabi for the first time since February, when negotiations took place in Geneva.Russia and Ukraine have held several rounds of failed talks during almost five years of war and hopes for peace are low. "We don't have any particular expectations," a senior Ukrainian official in Kyiv told AFP. - 'We don't want Yalta 2.0' - Trump last week floated a "very big agreement" on the war that will "involve all of Europe", stoking fears Washington would collaborate with Moscow on creating a new European security architecture.Shortly before launching its 2022 invasion, Moscow had issued an ultimatum to the West for NATO to rollback troops from Eastern Europe. The diplomat who issued the demand, Sergei Ryabkov, will for the first time be part of Moscow's delegation, which is headed by Putin's nationalistic aide Vladimir Medinsky.Kushner said Monday that a peace settlement will require direct Russia-Europe talks "on the broader security arrangements that affect them" and said the US "recognises difficult decisions ahead."These announcements have stoked fears in European capitals."For Europe, it is clear: we do not need to establish a new security architecture for Europe," German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Monday. He urged Moscow to "give up maximalist demands" and warned against any "negotiation show" in the UAE capital.Zelensky has warned of a "Yalta 2.0" referring to Western leaders dividing Europe with the USSR in 1945. According to Ukraine's chief negotiator Rustem Umerov, representatives from the UK, France, Germany and Italy, as well as NATO and EU officials will hold separate talks with Kyiv's representatives in Abu Dhabi. The Kremlin -- which has sought to keep Europe out of the talks -- said negotiations will remain "trilateral".A recent ceasefire in the Kherson region was "a very positive precedent", Ukrainian political expert Volodymyr Fesenko told AFP, predicting Kyiv will look for "de-escalation of the war through such local truces".Kushner and Witkoff have been accused by critics of being soft on Russia and US media have reported that the Americans are pushing large back-door business deals with Moscow. (Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Europe - alarmed by US President Donald Trump floating a deal with Moscow on European security ahead of the talks - will also send representatives to Abu Dhabi.
news.author: Agence France Presse

news.title: Iran war, cost of living drag Trump’s approval rating near career low: Survey
news.text: US President Donald Trump's approval rating remained close to the lowest level of his political career, with growing concerns over the cost of living weighing on his standing after the Republican Party's losses in last week's midterm elections.According to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted online across the US from November 6 to 9, 32 per cent of Americans approved of Trump's performance as president. The figure was unchanged from two previous Reuters/Ipsos polls conducted between late October and early November, and one percentage point above his career-low rating of 31 per cent recorded in mid-October.The poll surveyed 1,705 US adults and had a margin of error of approximately two percentage points.Trump's Republicans suffered losses in both chambers of Congress in the November 3 midterm elections.Although some races remain undecided, Democrats recorded their biggest House of Representatives victory since at least 2008 and flipped Senate seats in traditionally conservative states, including Kansas, South Carolina and Texas.Cost of living weighs on Trump's approvalThe poll found that only 21 per cent of Americans approved of Trump's handling of the cost of living, an issue that has emerged as a major concern for voters, Reuters reported.The war launched by the US President against Iran in February has sharply increased fuel prices and added pressure on household finances, according to the report.Trump's rating on the economy stood at 25 per cent, higher than his approval on the cost of living but well below his rating on immigration.Immigration remains a stronger areaHowever, Trump's approval rating on immigration policy stood at 38 per cent, considerably higher than his ratings on economic issues.Among Republican respondents, 81 per cent backed his approach to immigration, compared with 50 per cent who approved of his handling of the cost of living.Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has significantly expanded deportations of immigrants. Last week, he promoted Stephen Miller, a key architect of his immigration policies, to the position of White House chief of staff.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
news.summary: Donald Trump's approval rating stands at 32 per cent, close to his lowest in recent years. Concerns about the cost of living have significantly affected his standing among voters. The Republican Party experienced losses in both chambers of Congress during the midterm elections. Trump has taken action to address immigration, which resonates more positively with his supporters compared to his economic policies.

news.title: China hits $1 trillion trade surplus milestone for second year in a row
news.text: China's trade surplus crossed $1 trillion in the first 10 months of the year, as strong global demand for high-tech products, fuelled by the race to build artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure, helped offset weak domestic consumption.The surplus reached $1.04 trillion between January and October, according to customs data released on Tuesday.China has now recorded a trade surplus of more than $1 trillion for a second consecutive year, reaching the milestone a month earlier than in 2025.Exports rose 35.2% in October from a year earlier in US dollar terms, slightly below September's 36.3% increase but higher than the 33.5% growth forecast by economists in a Reuters poll.Imports grew 41.6%, accelerating from 31% in September and beating the poll's median forecast of 32%.Despite the stronger import growth, China's trade surplus narrowed to $105.3 billion in October from $133.5 billion in September.The export performance reflects China's growing reliance on overseas demand as subdued domestic consumption and a prolonged property market downturn weigh on its economy.The global AI investment boom has supported sales of Chinese technology products, including semiconductors and electronics, but the expanding surplus is also raising concerns among trading partners.AI demand supports exports, but trade tensions persistMuch of China's export growth this year has been driven by the global push to expand AI infrastructure. Analysts expect demand for Chinese technology products to remain strong into 2027, although the outlook will depend on how long the investment boom lasts.“The outlook for exports depends on how long the AI boom will last,” Macquarie analysts wrote, adding that exports could accelerate further in the fourth quarter before beginning to slow from the first quarter of 2027.Dave Chia, an economist at Moody's Analytics, also expects Chinese exports to remain strong through the rest of the year, led by electronics and automobiles.However, the expanding surplus could intensify trade tensions, particularly with the European Union.European leaders have called for further trade restrictions on China after reaching an agreement with Beijing to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to the bloc over the next few years.Since the measures have yet to take effect, manufacturers are expected to bring forward shipments, supporting exports in the near term.“The risk of additional tariffs and other trade barriers will remain elevated in 2027, particularly as Chinese manufacturers continue expanding their presence in overseas markets,” said Joe Peissel, lead macroeconomist at Trivium China.The US-China trade relationship also remains uncertain. Beijing on Monday officially announced a two-month extension of its trade truce with Washington, which was due to expire on November 10.However, China said last week that any expansion of its purchases of US agricultural goods would depend on the implementation of the agreed reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.China's trade surplus with the US narrowed slightly to $32.71 billion in October from $34.01 billion in September, but the gap remains a point of friction between the two economies.Trade is expected to feature prominently in the planned meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in Shenzhen later this month.The two leaders are expected to meet for the third time this year.Weak domestic demand adds to export dependenceThe strong export performance comes against the backdrop of subdued consumer spending in China. A prolonged downturn in the property market has weakened household wealth and confidence, leaving domestic demand under pressure.The weakness has also pushed Chinese manufacturers to look overseas for customers. Automobile exports maintained a solid pace of growth in October, while domestic vehicle sales recorded their 12th consecutive monthly decline, according to separate industry data.AP cited analysts who said overcapacity in several industries, excess domestic savings and weak domestic demand were pushing Chinese companies to sell more goods abroad. Alicia García-Herrero, chief economist for Asia Pacific at Natixis, said the situation was not sustainable.Businesses are also facing intense competition at home. Cinders Zhou, who sells eyewear for a manufacturer in the eastern Chinese city of Linhai, told AP that competition had increasingly centred on price as products across the industry became more similar.“It comes down to product quality, or rather the increasingly the lack of it across the industry, since there's significant homogenization,” Zhou said. “That has forced everyone to compete on price.”Greater dependence on overseas markets also leaves China's economy more exposed to a slowdown in global demand or further trade restrictions. Analysts have warned that any correction in the AI industry could hurt exports of chips and electronics.“If the AI boom slows or turns into a correction, lower chip and electronics prices and smaller shipping volumes would hit China's exports hard,” Chia said, according to AP.Oil imports fall despite supply concernsChina's oil imports fell 13.3% in October compared with a year earlier, although shipments reached their highest level since March as buyers sought supplies following disruptions to Middle East flows caused by the US-Israeli war on Iran.The trade figures come ahead of the APEC summit, where trade policy and tariffs are expected to be among the key issues in discussions between Trump and Xi. The two sides had previously proposed a $60 billion package of reciprocal tariff cuts following their September summit in Washington, including around $17 billion worth of US agricultural goods.While Chinese officials have maintained that Beijing is not seeking to expand its trade surplus and wants more balanced global trade, the latest figures underline the importance of overseas demand to the country's export-led growth.You use AI every day. news.summary: China's trade surplus surpassed $1 trillion in the first ten months, driven primarily by high-tech product demand. Exports increased significantly due to the global AI investment boom, although imports also grew faster than expected. Domestic consumption remains weak, which has pressured manufacturers to seek overseas markets for growth. Trade tensions with the European Union and the United States add complexity to China's export situation.
